Jiff 1.0: A datetime library for Rust
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
16:53:39 UTC
01:53:39 KST

Jiff is a datetime library for Rust that encourages you to jump into the pit of success. Jiff automatically handles many common problems related to daylight saving time by putting time zone handling front and center into the API. Jiff has already seen widespread adoption in the Rust ecosystem.
Jiff is pronounced like “gif” with a soft “g,” as in “gem.”
This blog announces the Jiff 1.0 release by giving a tour of its API.
Target audience: Rust programmers who need convenient datetime handling.
Table of Contents
The Jiff 1.0 Commitment
Jiff is already used in production in many projects: uv, Cargo, Starship, fd, Nushell, mise, Jujutsu, uutils/coreutils and even as the basis for a Temporal implementation in AWS LLRT. It is time to call it 1.0.
Unless some significant defect is found in Jiff’s API, my plan is to commit to Jiff 1.0 indefinitely. This is important because the intent is for Jiff to be an ecosystem building block that appears in the public API of other libraries. This makes Jiff an attractive public dependency, which means semver incompatible releases are likely to cause significant pain in the ecosystem. They will not be made lightly.
To see a list of breaking changes between Jiff 0.2 and Jiff 1.0, please consult the CHANGELOG.
Introduction
In programming, a datetime library’s core functionality rests at the intersection of a computer system’s concept of time and a human’s concept of time. The prevailing notion of system time is Unix time. A human’s concept of time is far more complex, but the most popular such model is the Gregorian calendar coupled with either a 12-hour or 24-hour clock. At the core of every datetime library rests some routine for converting between these concepts.
A datetime library typically provides much more than this. Indeed, datetime handling has historically been very difficult. My own belief is that the difficulty comes from poor modeling of the domain. Instead of encapsulating the complexity inside a reusable bundle of code, many datetime libraries pass some or all of the complexity on to its users. Jiff instead tries hard to encapsulate the complexity and make it difficult for users to do something wrong. (Jiff is not the first to do this!)
In this section of the blog, we’ll do some very basic introductions.
Follow Along
To follow along with the examples in this blog, create a new Cargo project
with dependencies on jiff and anyhow:
mkdir jiff-playground
cd jiff-playground
cargo init --bin
cargo add jiff anyhow
$EDITOR src/main.rs
Most examples are a complete self-contained Rust program. Just copy the code
and replace whatever is in src/main.rs. Then run the program:
cargo run
Terms
I am loath to present a dictionary. However, the datetime domain is littered with confusable terms, so I think it’s important to orient ourselves on a shared vocabulary. I’ve kept this section as small as possible. (Some terms, like “time zone,” are omitted here because they are best defined through exploration in the sections that follow.)
- Civil time: The time you see on your clock. And in general, the time that the humans in your approximate geographic vicinity also see. That is, civil time is a human coordinated agreement for communicating time in a particular geographic region. Civil time is also known as: local time, plain time, naive time, clock time and others.
- UTC: An abbreviation for Coordinated Universal Time; it is a time standard that serves as the basis for civil time around the world. It was originally intended to roughly correspond to mean solar time.
- TAI: An abbreviation for International Atomic Time; it is a time standard as measured by atomic clocks. It isn’t directly connected to mean solar time.
- Leap second: An adjustment to TAI to bring it closer to mean solar time and thus forming the basis of UTC.
- Unix time: UTC, but ignoring leap seconds.
TAI and leap seconds won’t be a feature of this blog, but they are listed here in order to convey the difference between Unix time and UTC.
The DateTime Onion
As a way to transition into some of the core types of Jiff, I’ve come to think
of its datetime types like an onion. In reverse order, we can build up
its layers all the way to a ZonedDateTime. So let’s start with more terms,
but this time, they are also types in Jiff:
- A civil::Date is a plain Gregorian date, unattached to any specific
location.
- A civil::Time is a plain time on a clock, to nanosecond precision,
unattached to any specific location.
- A civil::DateTime combines a civil::Date and a civil::Time to provide
both a Gregorian date and a time on a clock. It is also unattached to any
specific location.
- A Timestamp is an unambiguous specific instant in time regardless of
geographic location, represented as the number of nanoseconds since the Unix
epoch.
- A TimeZone is a set of rules for mapping a Timestamp to a civil::DateTime, and vice versa, in a specific geographic region.
- A ZonedDateTime combines a Timestamp, a civil::DateTime and a TimeZone to represent a specific instant in time in a specific geographic
location.
To make this a bit more concrete, we can see what this looks like in code. Since a time zone can map from a civil datetime to an instant in time, one way to create a zoned datetime requires only a civil datetime and a time zone:
use jiff::civil;
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let date = civil::date(2026, 11, 1);
    let time = civil::time(17, 30, 0, 0);
    let datetime = date.to_datetime(time);
    // zdt is an initialism for "ZonedDateTime"
    let zdt = datetime.in_tz("America/New_York")?;
    assert_eq!(zdt.timestamp().as_second(), 1793572200);
    Ok(())
}
Another way to create a zoned datetime requires only a timestamp and a time zone. This is because time zones can also map a timestamp to a particular civil datetime:
use jiff::{civil, Timestamp};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let timestamp = Timestamp::from_second(1793572200)?;
    let zdt = timestamp.in_tz("America/New_York")?;
    // This is a shortcut for creating a civil datetime.
    // The previous example spells it out a bit more verbosely
    // for clarity.
    let expected = civil::date(2026, 11, 1).at(17, 30, 0, 0);
    assert_eq!(zdt.datetime(), expected);
    Ok(())
}
Notice how we get the equivalent zoned datetime in both cases, but we come at it from different directions. In the first case, we start with a time that we might see on our clocks and calendars. In the second case, we start with a particular instant in time that we might get from a database or file system or some other system call.
Defining a time zone
There is one piece missing from the zoned datetime onion examples: the
time zone offset. An offset represents the amount of time one must
adjust UTC time in order to get civil time. For example, consider the time
2026-11-01T22:30:00 in UTC. In order to get the civil datetime for someone
living in New York, one would subtract 5 hours:
2026-11-01T22:30:00 - 05:00 = 2026-11-01T17:30:00
Indeed, every zoned datetime has an offset associated with it:
use jiff::{civil, tz, Timestamp};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let timestamp = Timestamp::from_second(1793572200)?;
    let zdt = timestamp.in_tz("America/New_York")?;
    assert_eq!(zdt.offset().seconds(), -(5 * 60 * 60));
    let dt = civil::date(2026, 11, 1).at(17, 30, 0, 0);
    let zdt = dt.in_tz("America/New_York")?;
    assert_eq!(zdt.offset(), tz::offset(-5));
    Ok(())
}
NOTE: The America/New_York string you see in the above example is an
IANA Time Zone Database Identifier. The IANA Time Zone Database is a
collection of time zone definitions that can be referenced by a short
identifier string. Examples: Australia/Sydney, Asia/Tokyo,
Europe/Berlin.
When a civil datetime is combined with an offset, then what you get is always an instant in time.
With the concept of an offset introduced, we can now give a more precise definition of a time zone. A time zone is a geographic region in which civil clocks agree and which provides the following:
- A mapping from an instant in time to an offset from UTC. The offset applied to an instant yields a civil datetime.
- A mapping from a civil datetime to a possibly ambiguous offset from UTC. The offset applied to a civil datetime yields an instant.
Both mappings have been demonstrated in prior examples, but the mapping from civil datetime to an offset seems to be rather complicated due to some potential ambiguity. When does that ambiguity arise? An ambiguous offset occurs when the civil datetime either doesn’t correspond to a valid clock time in this time zone (e.g., when clocks are moved ahead for daylight saving time) or where there could be multiple valid clock times (e.g., when clocks are moved backward for daylight saving time).
Let’s look at some examples. In this first example, we’ll take a look at times around the daylight saving time transition from summer time to standard time in New York. In New York, the clocks were “set back” by an hour at exactly 2AM. This caused the 1AM hour to repeat itself.
use jiff::{
    civil::date,
    tz::{offset, TimeZone},
};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let tz = TimeZone::get("America/New_York")?;
    // During summer time, New York's offset from UTC is -04:00.
    let zdt = date(2026, 11, 1).at(0, 30, 0, 0).to_zoned_datetime(tz.clone())?;
    assert_eq!(zdt.offset(), offset(-4));
    // During standard time, New York's offset from UTC is -05:00.
    let zdt = date(2026, 11, 1).at(2, 30, 0, 0).to_zoned_datetime(tz.clone())?;
    assert_eq!(zdt.offset(), offset(-5));
    // But what does 01:30AM mean? Is it the first repetition or the second?
    // Jiff automatically chooses the first by default.
    let zdt = date(2026, 11, 1).at(1, 30, 0, 0).to_zoned_datetime(tz.clone())?;
    assert_eq!(zdt.offset(), offset(-4));
    Ok(())
}
The above example shows how Jiff resolves the ambiguity when a “fold” occurs,
or when there is a time zone transition that moves the civil time backwards.
But we can actually dig down into lower level APIs to change how that ambiguity
is resolved. By default, Jiff uses a “compatible” strategy that always selects
the first repetition of a time in a fold. But other strategies can be selected
by using APIs on a TimeZone directly:
use jiff::{
    civil::date,
    tz::{offset, TimeZone},
};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let tz = TimeZone::get("America/New_York")?;
    let dt = date(2026, 11, 1).at(1, 30, 0, 0);
    // The same that Jiff uses by default.
    let zdt = tz.to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime(dt).compatible()?;
    assert_eq!(zdt.offset(), offset(-4));
    // Always selects the earlier datetime.
    // For a fold, this is the same as the
    // default "compatible" strategy.
    let zdt = tz.to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime(dt).earlier()?;
    assert_eq!(zdt.offset(), offset(-4));
    // Always selects the later datetime.
    // For a fold, this selects the second
    // occurrence of the 1AM hour!
    let zdt = tz.to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime(dt).later()?;
    assert_eq!(zdt.offset(), offset(-5));
    // Always returns an error when there
    // is any ambiguity.
    assert_eq!(
        tz.to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime(dt)
            .unambiguous()
            .unwrap_err()
            .to_string(),
        "error converting datetime to instant in time zone America/New_York: \
         datetime is ambiguous \
         since it falls into a fold between offsets -04 and -05",
    );
    Ok(())
}
The same idea applies to gaps, or time zone transitions where there’s some civil time that gets skipped on civil clocks. For example, on March 8, 2026 at 2AM, civil time skipped ahead to 3AM:
use jiff::{
    civil::date,
    tz::{offset, TimeZone},
};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let tz = TimeZone::get("America/New_York")?;
    let dt = date(2026, 3, 8).at(2, 30, 0, 0);
    // The "compatible" strategy selects
    // the later time in the case of gaps.
    let zdt = tz.to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime(dt).compatible()?;
    assert_eq!(zdt.offset(), offset(-4));
    // Always selects the earlier datetime.
    // For a gap, this selects the hour
    // before the gap.
    let zdt = tz.to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime(dt).earlier()?;
    assert_eq!(zdt.offset(), offset(-5));
    // Always selects the later datetime.
    // For a gap, this is the same as the
    // default "compatible" strategy.
    let zdt = tz.to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime(dt).later()?;
    assert_eq!(zdt.offset(), offset(-4));
    // Always returns an error when there
    // is any ambiguity.
    assert_eq!(
        tz.to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime(dt)
            .unambiguous()
            .unwrap_err()
            .to_string(),
        "error converting datetime to instant in time zone America/New_York: \
         datetime is ambiguous \
         since it falls into a gap between offsets -05 and -04",
    );
    Ok(())
}
Durations
There are two remaining core types, both representing some notion of a duration:
- Span is a powerful hybrid duration that combines both calendar units
(years, months, weeks, days) and physical time units (hours, minutes, seconds,
milliseconds, microseconds, nanoseconds). It is a beefy type that preserves the
individual unit values.
- SignedDuration is a signed version of std::time::Duration and always
corresponds to a 96-bit integer number of nanoseconds. It can only represent
physical time (units of hours or smaller) and not calendar units (units of days
or greater).
A Span is the preferred duration type to use whenever possible. Here’s a
simple example that shows how to get the number of days between two civil
dates:
use jiff::civil::date;
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let d1 = date(2024, 2, 1);
    let d2 = date(2024, 3, 1);
    let span = d2 - d1;
    assert_eq!(span.get_days(), 29);
    // or, equivalently:
    assert_eq!(d1.until(d2)?.get_days(), 29);
    // Flipping d1 and d2 gives the same result,
    // but negative.
    let span = d1 - d2;
    assert_eq!(span.get_days(), -29);
    Ok(())
}
Durations can also be added to dates:
use jiff::{civil::date, ToSpan};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let d1 = date(2024, 2, 1);
    // This convenient syntax comes from the
    // `ToSpan` extension trait.
    let span = 29.days();
    assert_eq!(d1.checked_add(span)?, date(2024, 3, 1));
    Ok(())
}
Generally speaking, whenever there is an operation involving a Span, there is
an equivalent operation available with SignedDuration:
use jiff::{civil::date, SignedDuration};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let dt1 = date(2024, 2, 1).at(17, 30, 0, 0);
    let sdur = SignedDuration::from_mins(90);
    assert_eq!(dt1.checked_add(sdur)?, date(2024, 2, 1).at(19, 0, 0, 0));
    Ok(())
}
Notice that in the above example, we actually switched from using a
civil::Date to a civil::DateTime. This was done to show how physical time
units can be added. But note that the same can be accomplished with a Span,
because it combines all units:
use jiff::{civil::date, ToSpan};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let dt1 = date(2024, 2, 1).at(17, 30, 0, 0);
    let span = 1.hour().minutes(30);
    assert_eq!(dt1.checked_add(span)?, date(2024, 2, 1).at(19, 0, 0, 0));
    // Calendar and physical time units can
    // be combined!
    let span = 1.month().hours(1).minutes(30);
    assert_eq!(dt1.checked_add(span)?, date(2024, 3, 1).at(19, 0, 0, 0));
    Ok(())
}
In brief, use a Span when you can. But when it’s too bulky or too slow, use
a SignedDuration. One of the key benefits of a Span is that since it
represents each unit value distinctly, one can preserve the original meaning
of a duration. For example, it’s common to represent the runtime of films in
minutes, even when the duration exceeds one hour. Indeed, a span of 2 hours
is a distinct span from a span of 120 minutes:
use jiff::ToSpan;
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let span1 = 2.hours();
    let span2 = 120.minutes();
    // This means the spans are distinct values
    // in memory.
    assert_ne!(span1.fieldwise(), span2.fieldwise());
    Ok(())
}
The Span::fieldwise routine converts a Span into a value whose units can
be compared in a field-by-field fashion. To compare spans based on the actual
physical duration they represent, use Span::compare:
let span1 = 2.hours();
let span2 = 120.minutes();
assert!(span1.compare(span2)?.is_eq());
This was a very brief introduction to durations in Jiff. They are a lot more powerful than what is shown here. You might even try playing with the examples above to explore its nooks and crannies. We’ll cover their API in more detail in a later section.
When should I use Jiff?
Jiff isn’t always the right thing to use. Sometimes you can get by with something simpler.
First and foremost, if you’re measuring the time something takes in a
program, you should almost certainly be using monotonic time. This is
available via std::time::Instant:
use std::time::{Duration, Instant};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let start = Instant::now();
    // do some serious work
    std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(1));
    let elapsed = Instant::now().duration_since(start);
    println!("{elapsed:?}");
    Ok(())
}
If you do need to compute elapsed time using your system clock, then Jiff is very convenient for that:
use std::time::Duration;
use jiff::Timestamp;
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    // assume `start` came from somewhere
    // over a network
    let start = Timestamp::now();
    std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(1));
    let elapsed = Timestamp::now().duration_since(start);
    println!("{elapsed}");
    Ok(())
}
But you don’t actually need Jiff for this. A std::time::SystemTime will
work perfectly fine:
use std::time::{Duration, SystemTime};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    // assume `start` came from somewhere
    // over a network
    let start = SystemTime::now();
    std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_secs(1));
    let elapsed = SystemTime::now().duration_since(start)?;
    println!("{elapsed:?}");
    Ok(())
}
Where Jiff starts to become useful is when you need something beyond just an
integer number of seconds since the Unix epoch. For example, some very hairy
math is required in order to convert a SystemTime into an RFC 3339 timestamp
like 2026-11-14T21:34:00Z.
As long as you can live in UTC completely, don’t care about local time and can work with Unix timestamps only, then the Rust standard library won’t steer you wrong.
Parsing and Formatting
Conversion to and from strings is a major part of Jiff. Jiff’s focus is primarily on interoperability via the following:
- RFC 3339 specifies a format for fixed offset instants in time, in terms of
a human readable civil datetime. For example, 2026-11-12T15:36:00-05:00. This
is the serialization format used by Timestamp.
- RFC 9557 extends and updates RFC 3339 to add time zone information.
For example, 2026-11-12T15:36:00-05:00[America/New_York]. This is the
serialization format used by ZonedDateTime.
- ISO 8601 covers mostly everything else, including durations and
civil datetimes. For example, P5Y3MT20H is an ISO 8601 duration and 2026-11-12T15:30:00 is an ISO 8601 civil datetime whose corresponding instant
in time is unknown.
What Jiff actually implements is the
Temporal RFC 9557 / ISO 8601 grammar for flexible parsing of datetimes from
strings. For most use cases, it suffices to think in terms of RFC 3339,
RFC 9557 or ISO 8601. But Jiff does support parsing strings that aren’t valid
in any of those three specifications. For example, 2026-11-12[America/New_York]
parses as if it was 2026-11-12T00:00:00[America/New_York].
In this section, we’ll take a tour of how Jiff does datetime formatting and printing.
FromStr and Display
Every datetime and duration type in Jiff implements the standard library
FromStr and Display traits. This means that it’s natural to parse
datetimes:
let ts: Timestamp = "2026-10-31T05:15:00Z".parse()?;
and print them:
println!("{ts}");
Parsing is flexible, so even if there are components missing, parsing still succeeds. For example, without minutes or seconds, those components default to zero:
let dt: civil::DateTime = "2026-10-31T05".parse()?;
assert_eq!(dt.to_string(), "2026-10-31T05:00:00");
Another example of flexible parsing is that if a string contains another date type, then one can parse that. For example, one can parse a date out of an ISO 8601 datetime:
let d: civil::Date = "2026-10-31T05:30".parse()?;
assert_eq!(d.to_string(), "2026-10-31");
A ZonedDateTime always uses RFC 9557 syntax, which includes the IANA time
zone identifier:
let zdt: ZonedDateTime = "2026-10-31T05:30[Australia/Sydney]".parse()?;
// While the string we parsed didn't have any offset,
// one was automatically added by consulting the time
// zone definition for the civil datetime provided.
assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2026-10-31T05:30:00+11:00[Australia/Sydney]");
If you want to print a zoned datetime using only RFC 3339 syntax, then you can do so by formatting the timestamp directly with the zoned datetime’s offset:
let zdt: ZonedDateTime = "2026-10-31T05:30[Australia/Sydney]".parse()?;
assert_eq!(
    zdt.timestamp().display_with_offset(zdt.offset()).to_string(),
    "2026-10-31T05:30:00+11:00",
);
The Span and SignedDuration types also support the FromStr and
Display traits via the ISO 8601 duration format. For example:
use jiff::{SignedDuration, Span};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let duration = "PT5H30M";
    let span: Span = duration.parse()?;
    assert_eq!(span.to_string(), "PT5H30M");
    let sdur: SignedDuration = duration.parse()?;
    assert_eq!(sdur.to_string(), "PT5H30M");
    Ok(())
}
Since a Span is a hybrid duration that also supports calendar units, it can
parse durations with calendar units and physical time units. A SignedDuration
can only parse durations with physical time units:
use jiff::{SignedDuration, Span};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let duration = "P11Y2M28DT5H30M";
    let span: Span = duration.parse()?;
    assert_eq!(span.to_string(), "P11Y2M28DT5H30M");
    let err = duration.parse::<SignedDuration>().unwrap_err();
    assert_eq!(
        err.to_string(),
        "parsing ISO 8601 duration in this context requires \
         that the duration contain a time component \
         and no components of days or greater",
    );
    Ok(())
}
The ISO 8601 duration format does, however, have some shortcomings that we’ll discuss in the next section.
The “friendly” Duration Format
Because ISO 8601 duration strings enjoy broad support, it is the default in
Jiff for both Span and SignedDuration. However, it has two important
shortcomings:
- It is difficult to read. For example, in P11Y2M28DT5H30M, the lack of
whitespace makes the unit values and the unit labels all run together.
- An ISO 8601 duration cannot unambiguously represent all possible Span values.
The second shortcoming is best seen with an example. Consider a Span that is
2000 milliseconds. If you convert this to an ISO 8601 duration string and then
parse it back, you end up with 2 seconds instead:
use jiff::{Span, ToSpan};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let original = 2000.milliseconds();
    assert_eq!(original.to_string(), "PT2S");
    let got: Span = "PT2S".parse()?;
    // The spans have different unit values!
    assert_eq!(original.get_seconds(), 0);
    assert_eq!(original.get_milliseconds(), 2000);
    assert_eq!(got.get_seconds(), 2);
    assert_eq!(got.get_milliseconds(), 0);
    Ok(())
}
This might not be desirable for cases where you want a span’s string format to faithfully represent all possible distinct values of a span.
For these two reasons, Jiff comes with its own bespoke “friendly” duration format. The friendly format is non-lossy and is meant to be easier to read for English speakers than the ISO 8601 duration format. Here are some examples that are all valid friendly durations:
40d
40 days
1y1d
1yr 1d
3d4h59m
3 days, 4 hours, 59 minutes
3d 4h 59m
2h30m
2h 30m
1mo
1w
1 week
1w4d
1 wk 4 days
1m
0.0021s
0s
0d
0 days
3 mins 34s 123ms
3 mins 34.123 secs
3 mins 34,123s
1y1mo1d1h1m1.1s
1yr 1mo 1day 1hr 1min 1.1sec
1 year, 1 month, 1 day, 1 hour, 1 minute 1.1 seconds
1 year, 1 month, 1 day, 01:01:01.1
Parsing a friendly duration is as easy as parsing an ISO 8601 duration: the
FromStr implementations on both Span and SignedDuration support ISO 8601
durations and friendly durations simultaneously:
let span: Span = "6y 10mo 3d 23h".parse()?;
// Recall that `Span::fieldwise` permits
// equality comparisons on `Span` in a
// unit-by-unit fashion.
assert_eq!(span.fieldwise(), 6.years().months(10).days(3).hours(23));
Printing a friendly duration does require a bit more effort, since it isn’t
the default. Instead of Span::to_string(), one can use the “alternative”
syntax via Rust’s formatting machinery:
let span = 2000.milliseconds();
// This also demonstrates that our unit
// values are preserved.
assert_eq!(format!("{span:#}"), "2000ms");
One can also use a lower level friendly printer to customize its output.
For example, here’s how to write a span in the friendly format to an existing
String using more spacing, longer unit labels and commas separating each
unit:
use jiff::{fmt::friendly, ToSpan};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    static PRINTER: friendly::SpanPrinter = friendly::SpanPrinter::new()
        .comma_after_designator(true)
        .spacing(friendly::Spacing::BetweenUnitsAndDesignators)
        .designator(friendly::Designator::Verbose);
    let span = 6.years().months(10).days(3).hours(23);
    let mut buf = String::new();
    PRINTER.print_span(&span, &mut buf)?;
    assert_eq!(buf, "6 years, 10 months, 3 days, 23 hours");
    Ok(())
}
See the jiff::fmt::friendly module for a lot more detail, including a
grammar that precisely specifies the format supported.
strptime and strftime
The POSIX strptime and POSIX strftime routines are far from the ideal
way to format and parse datetimes, but they are ubiquitous and most programmers
are familiar with them. Because of their ubiquity, and because of the utility
of being able to format and parse bespoke datetime formats, Jiff provides
implementations of these routines that are mostly POSIX compatible.
Every datetime type in Jiff comes with strptime and strftime routines.
For example, to parse a civil date in the US month/day/year format:
let date = civil::Date::strptime("%m/%d/%Y", "11/13/2026")?;
assert_eq!(date.to_string(), "2026-11-13");
Or to format a zoned datetime in a convenient to read representation for English speakers:
let zdt = civil::date(2026, 11, 13).at(17, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("Australia/Sydney")?;
assert_eq!(
    zdt.strftime("%a, %b %d, %Y %H:%M %Z").to_string(),
    "Fri, Nov 13, 2026 17:30 AEDT",
);
Callers can also use lower level APIs from jiff::fmt::strtime to get access
to each parsed component individually:
use jiff::{civil, fmt::strtime::BrokenDownTime};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let tm = BrokenDownTime::parse(
        "%a, %b %d, %Y %H:%M",
        "Fri, Nov 13, 2026 17:30",
    )?;
    assert_eq!(tm.weekday(), Some(civil::Weekday::Friday));
    assert_eq!(tm.month(), Some(11));
    assert_eq!(tm.day(), Some(13));
    assert_eq!(tm.year(), Some(2026));
    assert_eq!(tm.hour(), Some(17));
    assert_eq!(tm.minute(), Some(30));
    assert_eq!(tm.second(), None);
    Ok(())
}
The jiff::fmt module
While the above tour should cover most use cases, there are sometimes reasons
for exerting more control over parsing or formatting. Or for supporting
alternate formats like RFC 2822. The jiff::fmt module is meant to cover
these use cases at the cost of more complex APIs. For example, consider parsing
an RFC 2822 datetime string from a &[u8] (which lets callers avoid a UTF-8
validation check):
use jiff::fmt::rfc2822;
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    static PARSER: rfc2822::DateTimeParser = rfc2822::DateTimeParser::new();
    let data = b"Sat, 13 Jul 2024 15:09:59 -0400";
    let ts = PARSER.parse_timestamp(data)?;
    assert_eq!(ts.to_string(), "2024-07-13T19:09:59Z");
    Ok(())
}
Another example shows how to change the default disambiguation strategy when
the provided civil datetime is ambiguous. For example, Sydney, Australia moved
the clocks backwards at 2026-04-05T03:00:00 local time. That is, they went
from UTC offset +11 to UTC offset +10. So what happens if we try to parse
a time on the clock that is repeated as a result?
use jiff::ZonedDateTime;
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let zdt: ZonedDateTime = "2026-04-05T02:30[Australia/Sydney]".parse()?;
    assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2026-04-05T02:30:00+11:00[Australia/Sydney]");
    Ok(())
}
Here, the first occurrence of 02:30 is selected, just before Sydney leaves
daylight saving time. Now, the data itself can actually select the desired
offset:
use jiff::ZonedDateTime;
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let zdt: ZonedDateTime =
        "2026-04-05T02:30+11:00[Australia/Sydney]".parse()?;
    assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2026-04-05T02:30:00+11:00[Australia/Sydney]");
    let zdt: ZonedDateTime =
        "2026-04-05T02:30+10:00[Australia/Sydney]".parse()?;
    assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2026-04-05T02:30:00+10:00[Australia/Sydney]");
    Ok(())
}
But this happens because there is no ambiguity in the data. Since the offset
is supplied, the exact instant in time is known. Going back to
2026-04-05T02:30[Australia/Sydney], which is ambiguous because it could
refer to two different instants in time, how do we modify the strategy for
resolving that ambiguity? We can’t using the standard library FromStr trait,
so we instead have to construct our own parser manually, just like we did for
RFC 2822 parsing above. This example shows how to do that and all of the
different disambiguation options. Remember, UTC offset +11:00 corresponds to
the first occurrence of 2026-04-05T02:30 on the clocks of folks in Sydney
while UTC offset +10:00 corresponds to the second occurrence.
use jiff::{fmt::temporal::DateTimeParser, tz::Disambiguation};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let string = "2026-04-05T02:30[Australia/Sydney]";
    // "compatible" is the default strategy, which selects
    // the earlier time in a fold (usually moving from daylight
    // saving time to standard time) and the later time in a
    // gap (usually moving from standard time to daylight
    // saving time).
    let parser = DateTimeParser::new().disambiguation(Disambiguation::Compatible);
    let zdt = parser.parse_zoned_datetime(string)?;
    assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2026-04-05T02:30:00+11:00[Australia/Sydney]");
    // "earlier" always selects the first occurrence
    // in a fold, or the time before a gap.
    // So this is the same as compatible in this case,
    // since our civil time is in a fold.
    let parser = DateTimeParser::new().disambiguation(Disambiguation::Earlier);
    let zdt = parser.parse_zoned_datetime(string)?;
    assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2026-04-05T02:30:00+11:00[Australia/Sydney]");
    // "later" always selects the second occurrence
    // in a fold, or the time after a gap.
    // So this is different from "compatible" for a
    // fold. Notice that the UTC +10:00 offset is
    // chosen.
    let parser = DateTimeParser::new().disambiguation(Disambiguation::Later);
    let zdt = parser.parse_zoned_datetime(string)?;
    assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2026-04-05T02:30:00+10:00[Australia/Sydney]");
    // "reject" means that if the instant is ambiguous,
    // then an error is returned.
    let parser = DateTimeParser::new().disambiguation(Disambiguation::Reject);
    let err = parser.parse_zoned_datetime(string).unwrap_err();
    assert_eq!(
        err.to_string(),
        "error converting datetime to instant \
         in time zone Australia/Sydney: \
         datetime is ambiguous since it falls \
         into a fold between offsets +11 and +10",
    );
    Ok(())
}
The jiff::fmt module contains lots of other goodies that we won’t cover
here, including, but not limited to:
- The ability to format directly into an existing allocation.
- Parsing a datetime into its individual components.
- Helpers for serde integration.
Locale Sensitive Formatting via ICU4X Integration
No section on datetime formatting would be complete without addressing locales. In this context, a locale is a set of user preferences used for formatting datetimes. This is useful when you want to present a datetime to an end user that doesn’t expect standard formats from RFC 3339, RFC 9557 or ISO 8601.
Jiff itself does not provide any facilities for dealing with locales. Instead,
users can opt into this support via the ICU4X project. To make conversions
between Jiff and ICU4X, the jiff-icu integration crate can be used.
Here’s an example showing how to format a zoned datetime in the fr-LA locale:
(You’ll need to run cargo add icu jiff-icu to your project for this to work.)
use icu::{
    calendar::Iso,
    datetime::{fieldsets, DateTimeFormatter},
    locale::locale,
    time::{zone::models::AtTime, TimeZoneInfo},
};
use jiff::ZonedDateTime;
use jiff_icu::ConvertFrom as _;
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    // Firstly, do a conversion from Jiff's zoned datetime to ICU's.
    let jiff_zdt: ZonedDateTime =
        "2024-09-10T23:37:20-04[America/New_York]".parse()?;
    let icu_zdt =
        icu::time::ZonedDateTime::<Iso, TimeZoneInfo<AtTime>>::convert_from(
            &jiff_zdt,
        );
    // Second, create a datetime formatter for the fr-LA locale:
    let formatter = DateTimeFormatter::try_new(
        locale!("fr-LA").into(),
        fieldsets::YMDET::medium().with_zone(fieldsets::zone::SpecificLong),
    )?;
    // Thirdly, format the zoned datetime.
    assert_eq!(
        formatter.format(&icu_zdt).to_string(),
        "mar. 10 sept. 2024, 23:37:20 heure d’été de l’Est nord-américain",
    );
    Ok(())
}
The ICU4X API has a lot of options for customizing datetime formatting. Exploring it further is outside the scope of this blog.
Date Manipulation
Jiff provides many methods on its datetime types to make using them as comfortable and error-free as possible.
Date Basics
Every datetime type provides a new constructor that lets callers build it
from its constituent parts. In most cases, this constructor is fallible. For
example:
use jiff::civil::Date;
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let d = Date::new(2024, 2, 29)?;
    // All datetime types have convenient
    // accessors for each of their components.
    assert_eq!(d.year(), 2024);
    assert_eq!(d.month(), 2);
    assert_eq!(d.day(), 29);
    let err = Date::new(2025, 2, 29).unwrap_err();
    assert_eq!(
        err.to_string(),
        "parameter 'day' for `2025-02` is invalid, must be in range `1..=28`",
    );
    Ok(())
}
Because creating dates is so common, there is a shorthand for doing so when you know the inputs are valid:
let d = const { civil::date(2024, 2, 29) };
assert_eq!(d.year(), 2024);
assert_eq!(d.month(), 2);
assert_eq!(d.day(), 29);
That is, civil::date is a const function that will panic if its inputs are
invalid. It should only be used with inputs that are known to be valid.
It would, for example, be inappropriate to use this with user provided values.
Because of the const block above, if you try to provide invalid values,
you’ll get a compiler error.
For datetime types that represent an instant in time (i.e., ZonedDateTime and
Timestamp), there is also a now() constructor for getting the current time:
use jiff::{Timestamp, ZonedDateTime};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let now = Timestamp::now();
    println!("{now}");
    // Example output: 2026-11-15T14:17:21.80099287Z
    // This will automatically fetch your system's configured time zone.
    let now = ZonedDateTime::now();
    println!("{now}");
    // Example output: 2026-11-15T09:17:21.80102125-05:00[America/New_York]
    Ok(())
}
In addition to constructors, new date values can be constructed from old
date values using the Date::with API:
let d1 = const { civil::date(2024, 2, 29) };
// This API doesn't break just because 31
// is supplied before a month that has 31
// days. Any order is fine! This is because
// errors are deferred until `build()` is
// called.
let d2 = d1.with().day(31).month(3).build()?;
assert_eq!(d2.to_string(), "2024-03-31");
Once you have a date, there are oodles of APIs available:
let d = civil::date(2025, 7, 10);
assert_eq!(d.weekday(), civil::Weekday::Thursday);
assert_eq!(d.first_of_year(), civil::date(2025, 1, 1));
assert_eq!(d.last_of_year(), civil::date(2025, 12, 31));
assert_eq!(d.first_of_month(), civil::date(2025, 7, 1));
assert_eq!(d.last_of_month(), civil::date(2025, 7, 31));
assert_eq!(d.yesterday()?, civil::date(2025, 7, 9));
assert_eq!(d.tomorrow()?, civil::date(2025, 7, 11));
Moreover, because of the datetime onion, all of these
APIs are also available on civil::DateTime and ZonedDateTime:
let create_zdt =
    |date: civil::Date| -> Result<ZonedDateTime, jiff::Error> {
        date.at(0, 0, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")
    };
let zdt = create_zdt(civil::date(2025, 7, 10))?;
assert_eq!(zdt.weekday(), civil::Weekday::Thursday);
assert_eq!(zdt.first_of_year()?, create_zdt(civil::date(2025, 1, 1))?);
assert_eq!(zdt.last_of_year()?, create_zdt(civil::date(2025, 12, 31))?);
assert_eq!(zdt.first_of_month()?, create_zdt(civil::date(2025, 7, 1))?);
assert_eq!(zdt.last_of_month()?, create_zdt(civil::date(2025, 7, 31))?);
assert_eq!(zdt.yesterday()?, create_zdt(civil::date(2025, 7, 9))?);
assert_eq!(zdt.tomorrow()?, create_zdt(civil::date(2025, 7, 11))?);
These routines on ZonedDateTime also take time zone transitions into account.
For example, ZonedDateTime knows that tomorrow() doesn’t always add 24
hours:
// On 2024-11-03 at 2AM in New York, time was rolled
// back 1 hour in the transition from daylight saving
// time to standard time. That means 2024-11-03 was
// actually 25 hours long in New York.
let zdt =
    civil::date(2024, 11, 2).at(17, 25, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
let tomorrow = zdt.tomorrow()?;
assert_eq!(tomorrow.datetime(), civil::date(2024, 11, 3).at(17, 25, 0, 0));
// The physical time difference between them is 25 hours!
let span = tomorrow - zdt;
assert_eq!(format!("{span:#}"), "25h");
NOTE: We’ll talk about date arithmetic in the next section.
When ZonedDateTime::tomorrow() (among other APIs that produce a
ZonedDateTime) would land in a gap or a fold, the “compatible” disambiguation
strategy is chosen automatically:
// For a zoned datetime that lands
// in a fold, the earlier instant is
// chosen by default.
let zdt =
    civil::date(2024, 11, 2).at(1, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
let tomorrow = zdt.tomorrow()?;
assert_eq!(
    tomorrow.to_string(),
    "2024-11-03T01:30:00-04:00[America/New_York]"
);
// And for a gap, the later instant
// is chosen by default.
let zdt =
    civil::date(2024, 3, 9).at(2, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
let tomorrow = zdt.tomorrow()?;
assert_eq!(
    tomorrow.to_string(),
    "2024-03-10T03:30:00-04:00[America/New_York]"
);
To override this behavior, you can drop down to civil datetimes, perform the
operation, and then use TimeZone::to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime to control the
exact disambiguation strategy:
// For a zoned datetime that lands
// in a fold, the earlier instant is
// chosen by default. But let's say
// we want the later instant.
let zdt =
    civil::date(2024, 11, 2).at(1, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
let tomorrow = zdt
    .time_zone()
    .to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime(zdt.datetime().tomorrow()?)
    .later()?;
assert_eq!(
    tomorrow.to_string(),
    // Notice that the offset is now -05,
    // which corresponds to the later
    // instant.
    "2024-11-03T01:30:00-05:00[America/New_York]"
);
There are a few other methods of note on date types that are worth mentioning.
First is the ability to query for things like, “The Thursday after next” or
“The last Sunday of the month.” The former can be answered by the nth_weekday
API:
let zdt1 = civil::date(2024, 7, 10).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
assert_eq!(zdt1.weekday(), civil::Weekday::Wednesday);
// Not this Thursday, but the next!
let zdt2 = zdt1.nth_weekday(2, civil::Weekday::Thursday)?;
assert_eq!(zdt2.weekday(), civil::Weekday::Thursday);
assert_eq!(zdt2.date(), civil::date(2024, 7, 18));
While the latter can be answered by the nth_weekday_of_month API:
let zdt1 = civil::date(2024, 7, 10).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
assert_eq!(zdt1.weekday(), civil::Weekday::Wednesday);
// The last Sunday of this month.
let zdt2 = zdt1.nth_weekday_of_month(-1, civil::Weekday::Sunday)?;
assert_eq!(zdt2.weekday(), civil::Weekday::Sunday);
assert_eq!(zdt2.date(), civil::date(2024, 7, 28));
Finally, users can access a convenient time series iterator via series:
use jiff::{civil, ToSpan};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let start = civil::date(2024, 7, 10).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
    let mut dates = vec![];
    // Every week for 8 weeks.
    for zdt in start.series(1.week()).take(8) {
        dates.push(zdt);
    }
    assert_eq!(
        dates,
        vec![
            civil::date(2024, 7, 10).in_tz("America/New_York")?,
            civil::date(2024, 7, 17).in_tz("America/New_York")?,
            civil::date(2024, 7, 24).in_tz("America/New_York")?,
            civil::date(2024, 7, 31).in_tz("America/New_York")?,
            civil::date(2024, 8, 7).in_tz("America/New_York")?,
            civil::date(2024, 8, 14).in_tz("America/New_York")?,
            civil::date(2024, 8, 21).in_tz("America/New_York")?,
            civil::date(2024, 8, 28).in_tz("America/New_York")?,
        ]
    );
    Ok(())
}
All of these methods are also available on civil::Date and
civil::DateTime, which should make it very natural to move between them.
Date Arithmetic
All datetime types in Jiff support adding and subtracting durations, and
finding the span of time between two datetime values. Let’s start with a
civil::Date:
use jiff::{civil, ToSpan};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let d1 = civil::date(2024, 7, 30);
    let d2 = d1 + 2.days();
    assert_eq!(d2, civil::date(2024, 8, 1));
    Ok(())
}
Here we make use of the std::ops::Add trait implementation for civil::Date.
The downside of using this, though, is that if the date value goes out of
range, then it panics. That may or may not be acceptable. But if you’re dealing
with user inputs, then you should use Date::checked_add instead:
use jiff::{civil, ToSpan};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let d1 = civil::date(2024, 7, 30);
    let d2 = d1.checked_add(2.days())?;
    assert_eq!(d2, civil::date(2024, 8, 1));
    Ok(())
}
Let’s take a look at a few other examples involving months and years:
let d = civil::date(2024, 5, 31);
assert_eq!(d.checked_add(1.month())?, civil::date(2024, 6, 30));
assert_eq!(d.checked_add(2.months())?, civil::date(2024, 7, 31));
let d = civil::date(2025, 1, 31);
assert_eq!(d.checked_add(1.month())?, civil::date(2025, 2, 28));
let d = civil::date(2024, 2, 29);
let span = 1.year().months(2).days(5);
assert_eq!(d.checked_add(span)?, civil::date(2025, 5, 4));
As with other methods on Date, they are also available on ZonedDateTime:
let d = civil::date(2024, 5, 31).at(13, 45, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
assert_eq!(
    d.checked_add(1.month())?,
    civil::date(2024, 6, 30).at(13, 45, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?
);
If we take a look at the type signature for ZonedDateTime::checked_add, we
can see that it’s actually polymorphic:
pub fn checked_add<A: Into<ZonedDateTimeArithmetic>>(
    &self,
    duration: A,
) -> Result<ZonedDateTime, Error>
Specifically, it accepts anything that can be converted into a
ZonedDateTimeArithmetic. In this case, there are From trait
implementations for the following types:
This means that ZonedDateTime::checked_add can accept any one of these
duration values:
use jiff::{civil, SignedDuration};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let d =
        civil::date(2024, 5, 31).at(13, 45, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
    assert_eq!(
        d.checked_add(SignedDuration::from_mins(45))?,
        civil::date(2024, 5, 31).at(14, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?
    );
    Ok(())
}
This type of polymorphism is common in Jiff. Here, it is merely used to provide a convenient way to use multiple duration types. But as we’ll see, it’s also used to provide an extension point for configuration options that control how the operation works.
In addition to adding or subtracting durations from datetime values, one can also compute the duration between two datetime values. For example, to get the number of days between two dates:
use jiff::{civil, ToSpan};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let d1 = civil::date(2024, 5, 31);
    let d2 = civil::date(2024, 9, 30);
    assert_eq!(d2 - d1, 122.days().fieldwise());
    Ok(())
}
Similarly, we can use Date::until to compute the span between dates:
let d1 = civil::date(2024, 5, 31);
let d2 = civil::date(2024, 9, 30);
assert_eq!(d1.until(d2)?, 122.days().fieldwise());
Like with Date::checked_add, this routine is also available at
ZonedDateTime::until:
let zdt1 = civil::date(2024, 5, 31).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
let zdt2 = civil::date(2024, 9, 30).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
assert_eq!(zdt1.until(&zdt2)?, 2928.hours().fieldwise());
Notice though that hours, instead of days, are returned. This is because two
ZonedDateTime values might be in different time zones. Since a ZonedDateTime
is fundamentally an instant in time, and because days might be of varying length
depending on the time zone, defaulting to hours as the largest possible unit
means subtracting two zoned datetimes will always succeed. However, we can
request larger units in the duration returned by passing additional options.
Notably, ZonedDateTime::until is polymorphic:
pub fn until<'a, A: Into<ZonedDateTimeDifference<'a>>>(
    &self,
    other: A,
) -> Result<Span, Error>
That is, callers aren’t just limited to passing a ZonedDateTime here, but
anything that can be converted to a ZonedDateTimeDifference. Here is
one such example, where we can override the largest units returned in the
duration:
use jiff::{civil, ToSpan, Unit};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let zdt1 = civil::date(2024, 5, 31).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
    let zdt2 = civil::date(2024, 9, 30).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
    assert_eq!(
        zdt1.until((Unit::Month, &zdt2))?,
        3.months().days(30).fieldwise()
    );
    Ok(())
}
A ZonedDateTimeDifference provides much more powerful configuration options
for rounding the span returned. Take this example, which produces a span with
many unit values:
use jiff::{civil::date, ToSpan, Unit};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let zdt1 =
        date(2024, 5, 15).at(14, 30, 54, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
    let zdt2 = date(2024, 5, 31)
        .at(19, 13, 27, 123_456_789)
        .in_tz("America/New_York")?;
    assert_eq!(
        zdt1.until((Unit::Day, &zdt2))?,
        16.days()
            .hours(4)
            .minutes(42)
            .seconds(33)
            .milliseconds(123)
            .microseconds(456)
            .nanoseconds(789)
            .fieldwise(),
    );
    Ok(())
}
This might be too much precision to show to an end user. Instead, perhaps
we’d like to round the span to the nearest half-hour. We can do this by
building a ZonedDateTimeDifference explicitly and configuring its options:
use jiff::{civil::date, RoundMode, ToSpan, Unit, ZonedDateTimeDifference};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let zdt1 =
        date(2024, 5, 15).at(14, 30, 54, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
    let zdt2 = date(2024, 5, 31)
        .at(19, 13, 27, 123_456_789)
        .in_tz("America/New_York")?;
    let difference = ZonedDateTimeDifference::new(&zdt2)
        .largest(Unit::Day)
        .smallest(Unit::Minute)
        .increment(30)
        .mode(RoundMode::HalfExpand);
    assert_eq!(
        zdt1.until(difference)?,
        16.days().hours(4).minutes(30).fieldwise(),
    );
    Ok(())
}
Note also that rounding a span takes time zone transitions like daylight saving
time into account. For example, let’s take 2024-11-02 17:30 and
2024-11-03 04:45 in New York. Because New York stopped daylight saving time
at 2AM on 2024-11-03, the amount of physical time between them is 12 hours and
15 minutes:
let zdt1 = date(2024, 11, 2).at(17, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
let zdt2 = date(2024, 11, 3).at(4, 45, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
assert_eq!(zdt2 - zdt1, 12.hours().minutes(15).fieldwise());
Normally, if we rounded to the nearest day, this would round up to 1 day. But since the midpoint of this particular day is actually 12 hours and 30 minutes, this duration will round down to 0 days when we request it:
use jiff::{civil::date, RoundMode, ToSpan, Unit, ZonedDateTimeDifference};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let zdt1 = date(2024, 11, 2).at(17, 30, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
    let zdt2 = date(2024, 11, 3).at(4, 45, 0, 0).in_tz("America/New_York")?;
    let difference = ZonedDateTimeDifference::new(&zdt2)
        .largest(Unit::Day)
        .smallest(Unit::Day)
        .mode(RoundMode::HalfExpand);
    assert_eq!(zdt1.until(difference)?, 0.days().fieldwise());
    Ok(())
}
Next we’ll continue our discussion of rounding, but when applied to datetimes themselves.
Date Rounding
Date rounding in Jiff is limited to units of days or lower. Therefore, it’s
only available on ZonedDateTime, Timestamp, civil::DateTime,
civil::Time but not civil::Date.
A common example for rounding a datetime is to reduce precision. For example, a system clock might provide nanosecond precision, but maybe we only care about the nearest half-hour:
use jiff::{civil::date, Unit};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let zdt = date(2024, 11, 2)
        .at(17, 46, 20, 123_456_789)
        .in_tz("America/New_York")?;
    assert_eq!(
        zdt.to_string(),
        "2024-11-02T17:46:20.123456789-04:00[America/New_York]"
    );
    // Round to the nearest half hour.
    let rounded = zdt.round((Unit::Minute, 30))?;
    assert_eq!(
        rounded.to_string(),
        "2024-11-02T18:00:00-04:00[America/New_York]"
    );
    Ok(())
}
As with rounding spans, rounding a ZonedDateTime is aware of time zone
transitions:
let zdt = date(2024, 11, 3)
    .at(11, 45, 20, 123_456_789)
    .in_tz("America/New_York")?;
// Round to the nearest day.
let rounded = zdt.round(Unit::Day)?;
assert_eq!(
    rounded.to_string(),
    "2024-11-04T00:00:00-05:00[America/New_York]"
);
Notice that in the above example, our time of 11:45AM is before noon, yet the result still rounds up to the next day. This is because the midpoint for this day is 11:30AM since, by 11:30AM, 12.5 hours have already elapsed because of the repeated 1AM hour in the move away from daylight saving time in New York.
Other Calendars
Jiff itself doesn’t support any calendars other than the proleptic Gregorian
calendar. One can instead use the ICU4X crate to work in non-Gregorian
calendars, and convert between datetime types using the jiff-icu crate:
(Use cargo add icu jiff-icu to make this example work.)
use icu::{
    calendar::{types::Month, Date as IcuDate},
    time::{DateTime as IcuDateTime, Time as IcuTime},
};
use jiff::civil::DateTime;
use jiff_icu::ConvertTryFrom as _;
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    // Firstly, create an ICU datetime using the Hebrew calendar.
    let datetime = IcuDateTime {
        date: IcuDate::try_new_hebrew_v2(5785, Month::new(5), 4)?,
        time: IcuTime::try_new(17, 30, 0, 0)?,
    };
    // Secondly, convert it to a civil datetime.
    // This will automatically use ICU to convert
    // the date from the Hebrew calendar to the
    // Gregorian (or ISO) calendar.
    let zdt = DateTime::convert_try_from(datetime)?;
    assert_eq!(zdt.to_string(), "2025-02-02T17:30:00");
    Ok(())
}
The ICU4X API supports many more calendars.
Which DateTime Type Do I Use?
There are 3 potentially confusable datetime types in Jiff:
When should you use each one versus the other?
To a first approximation, if you can use a ZonedDateTime, then that is
probably the type you want to reach for. It represents a specific instant in
time in a particular geographic location. That is, it has both a Timestamp
and a TimeZone.
If you only ever need to work in UTC or just deal with system time, then a
Timestamp is probably the right choice. This is useful for representing a
specific instant in time that is not connected to any time zone.
A civil::DateTime is useful in contexts where you don’t care about a specific
instant in time and when calcuations should be done independent of time zone.
For example, when parsing datetime information from a user interface datetime
picker.
Remember that both a civil::DateTime and a Timestamp can be converted to a
ZonedDateTime by supplying a time zone.
Span Manipulation
We’ve already seen how to add spans to datetime values and how to get spans
as a difference between datetime values. But we haven’t yet explored the APIs
available on a Span itself.
First and foremost, we can build a Span through its constructor, which
returns a Span with all of its units set to 0:
use jiff::Span;
let span = Span::new();
A Span is both Copy and immutable. We can create new spans through method
chaining:
let span = Span::new().hours(1).minutes(30);
assert_eq!(span.to_string(), "PT1H30M");
Or we can use the ToSpan convenience trait, which adds methods on integer
types for constructing spans:
use jiff::ToSpan;
let span = 1.hour().minutes(30);
assert_eq!(span.to_string(), "PT1H30M");
Note though that methods like Span::hours and ToSpan::hours will panic
when the integer is outside the limits of what Span supports. This is fine
when your spans are literals in your program, since a panic would indicate a
bug. But if your inputs come from an end user, it’s better to use fallible
methods:
let span = Span::new().try_hours(1)?.try_minutes(30)?;
assert_eq!(span.to_string(), "PT1H30M");
Spans preserve each individual unit value. This means that 90 minutes and 1 hour 30 minutes, while they represent the same duration, are actually different values in memory:
let span1 = 1.hour().minutes(30);
let span2 = 90.minutes();
assert_eq!(span1.to_string(), "PT1H30M");
assert_eq!(span2.to_string(), "PT90M");
This permits callers maximum flexibility when it comes to representing
durations. This makes it possible to represent durations in a specific unit
even when they add up to larger units. For example, the runtime duration of
films is typically conveyed in minutes, even when the runtime exceeds one hour.
This can be adjusted programmatically using Span::round:
use jiff::{SpanRound, ToSpan, Unit};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let span1 = 1.hour().minutes(30);
    let span2 = span1.round(SpanRound::new().largest(Unit::Minute))?;
    assert_eq!(span2.to_string(), "PT90M");
    Ok(())
}
You can go the other way as well:
use jiff::{SpanRound, ToSpan, Unit};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let span1 = 90.minutes();
    let span2 = span1.round(SpanRound::new().largest(Unit::Hour))?;
    assert_eq!(span2.to_string(), "PT1H30M");
    Ok(())
}
Neither of these examples do actual rounding, despite the name of the API. Instead, since we’re only setting the largest unit, this API is doing unit balancing. Unit balancing is when all unit values rollover into larger units up until the largest configured unit. This works even for calendar units too, but you need to provide a relative date:
use jiff::{civil, SpanRound, ToSpan, Unit};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let span = 2756.hours();
    let dt = civil::date(2020, 1, 1).at(0, 0, 0, 0);
    let round = SpanRound::new().largest(Unit::Year).relative(dt);
    assert_eq!(span.round(round)?.to_friendly(), "3mo 23d 20h");
    Ok(())
}
Without a relative date, it’s not possible to know how many hours are in a single month. That is, once calendar units are involved, a span cannot be interpreted as a physical duration of time until some context is applied.
The same even applies to days themselves, since days can sometimes be more or less than 24 hours. Take the above example. What happens if we use a zoned datetime as our relative date instead?
use jiff::{civil, SpanRound, ToSpan, Unit};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let span = 2756.hours();
    let zdt = civil::date(2020, 1, 1).at(0, 0, 0, 0).in_tz("Europe/Rome")?;
    let round = SpanRound::new().largest(Unit::Year).relative(&zdt);
    assert_eq!(span.round(round)?.to_friendly(), "3mo 23d 21h");
    Ok(())
}
Notice that the duration’s hour component changed from 20 to 21. Why?
Because we started with 2756 hour in both cases and because 2020-03-29 in
Rome was only 23 hours long (in a move from standard time to daylight saving
time). That means that one of those days in 3mo 23d was only 23 hours long.
So an extra hour needed to be added to make up for it.
The round API can also do actual rounding:
use jiff::{SpanRound, ToSpan, Unit};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let span = 2.hours().minutes(30);
    let round = SpanRound::new().smallest(Unit::Hour);
    assert_eq!(span.round(round)?.to_friendly(), "3h");
    Ok(())
}
You can also change its rounding mode from the default (“half-expand”, or like you were taught rounding in school) to truncation (or one of several other modes):
use jiff::{RoundMode, SpanRound, ToSpan, Unit};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let span = 2.hours().minutes(30);
    let round = SpanRound::new().smallest(Unit::Hour).mode(RoundMode::Trunc);
    assert_eq!(span.round(round)?.to_friendly(), "2h");
    Ok(())
}
One can also specify a rounding increment to round to the nearest unit value. For example, to the nearest half-hour:
use jiff::{SpanRound, ToSpan, Unit};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let span = 2.hours().minutes(31);
    let round = SpanRound::new().smallest(Unit::Minute).increment(30);
    assert_eq!(span.round(round)?.to_friendly(), "2h 30m");
    Ok(())
}
Because a Span value cannot easily be compared correctly based purely on its
value in memory, a dedicated comparison Span::compare routine is provided:
let span1 = 2.hours();
let span2 = 120.minutes();
assert!(span1.compare(span2)?.is_eq());
Also, one can convert a Span to a floating point value in terms of any unit.
For example:
use jiff::{ToSpan, Unit};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let span = 90.minutes();
    assert_eq!(span.total(Unit::Hour)?, 1.5);
    Ok(())
}
Converting to calendar units requires a relative date for the same reasons discussed above:
use jiff::{civil, ToSpan, Unit};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let span = 24.hours();
    assert_eq!(
        span.total((Unit::Month, civil::date(2026, 6, 1)))?,
        0.03333333333333333
    );
    assert_eq!(
        span.total((Unit::Month, civil::date(2026, 7, 1)))?,
        0.03225806451612903
    );
    Ok(())
}
Conclusion
So far, we’ve explored a good chunk of Jiff’s API. We didn’t talk about every nook and cranny, but I think we’ve covered the most important pieces.
We’ll wrap up by briefly discussing motivation and inspiration.
Motivation
Whenever I needed datetime handling in Rust, I always got confused. Should I
use chrono or time? How do I get my local time from a timestamp? How do I
use my system’s time zone database? How do I do calendar arithmetic?
Before I started working on Jiff, this confusion got annoying enough for me to
consider writing my own crate. I felt like the APIs of both chrono and time
could be improved upon. I personally found the domain quite interesting and so
set out to build something better.
Why not improve on an existing solution, like chrono or time, instead of
adding yet another choice into the ecosystem? I do think there are material
downsides of having too many choices, but I had concluded that both chrono
and time (in 2024) had reached a local maximum. Moreover, in 2024, I was not
an expert in datetime handling. It took building a datetime library to become
one. So convincing crate maintainers to go in a radically different direction
would have been a tall order.
Jiff’s design and comparison documentation contain much more detail
regarding the motivation and specific examples between Jiff, chrono and
time.
Inspiration
Jiff is heavily inspired by Temporal, which is JavaScript’s standard library solution for date and time management. Jiff inherits API design, functionality and even parsing/formatting of datetime values. Note though that Jiff is not and does not aim to be a 100% compatible implementation of the Temporal specification. Jiff is meant to be a Rust ecosystem library first and foremost.
With that said, if you’re familiar with Temporal and Rust, then it’s likely you’ll find Jiff to be a relatively straightforward translation of Temporal’s API to Rust. This example shows how to use Temporal to round a calendar span to the nearest number of days relative to a date:
const duration = Temporal.Duration.from({ months: 1, days: 1, hours: 1 });
const roundedDuration = duration.round({
  largestUnit: "days",
  smallestUnit: "days",
  relativeTo: Temporal.PlainDateTime.from("2022-01-01"),
});
console.log(roundedDuration); // "P32D"
And here’s the equivalent operation in Jiff:
use jiff::{SpanRound, ToSpan, Unit};
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let span = 1.month().days(1).hours(1);
    let rounded_span = span.round(
        SpanRound::new()
            .largest(Unit::Day)
            .smallest(Unit::Day)
            .relative("2022-01-01".parse::<jiff::civil::Date>()?),
    )?;
    assert_eq!(rounded_span.to_string(), "P32D");
    Ok(())
}
The main difference between these examples is that Jiff’s duration type is
named Span instead of Duration. This was done to avoid confusion with
Rust’s standard library std::time::Duration type.
Here are some other differences:
- Temporal’s Instant type in Jiff is named Timestamp in order to avoid
confusion with Rust’s standard library std::time::Instant type.
- Temporal’s “plain” date and time types are called “civil” in Jiff.
- Jiff only supports the Gregorian calendar.
- Jiff’s datetime range only extends to +/- 9999, whereas Temporal’s range is larger.
It’s easy to say that without Temporal, Jiff wouldn’t exist in its current form today.

Microsoft Blames Monster Email Outage On Software Defect Introduced In July Fix
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
16:30:00 UTC
01:30:00 KST

Microsoft Blames Monster Email Outage On Software Defect Introduced In July Fix (theregister.com) 34
			
		 	
				Microsoft says last week's massive Microsoft 365 outage was caused by a software defect introduced in a July update that remained dormant until a Teams failover and a simultaneous 14% reduction in gateway capacity triggered a cascading failure. More than 80% of the affected gateway servers became unresponsive at the outage's worst point, and because the months-old change could not simply be rolled back, engineers spent roughly 15 hours developing and deploying a patch that restored the previous code path. The Register reports:  According to a preliminary post incident report published by Microsoft on November 15, the defect was introduced in July 2026. The update looked fine at the time, Microsoft says, having passed load testing and been deployed without any impact. However, the testing wasn't good enough. Microsoft's report states: "Our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores." The defect caused "lock contention inside an internal Windows process which caused the machine's resources (CPU & memory) to be exhausted."
"The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware." The fix containing the defect was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 network gateway servers. Then two things happened at once. Teams failed over to the "primary" gateway that supports Exchange Online, creating a surge in load that was not, in itself, particularly unusual. At the same time, almost 14 percent of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service, which wasn't a problem by itself either: it was on its way to being restored and, according to Microsoft, "the service had sufficient capacity headroom." Together, they pushed the gateway into the defect and chaos ensued. It was a classic cascading failure scenario. When a server loses connectivity, traffic gets routed to the next healthy endpoint. Which encountered the same problem. So traffic was rerouted again and... you can see where this was going. Within two hours, the defect was encountered across Microsoft's fleet. "At its lowest," the report states, "more than 80 percent of servers were unresponsive."
So, what to do? Bringing servers back to service didn't help -- they were immediately overwhelmed and fell over again. "Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state." A straightforward rollback was also not possible because the defect was months old. Instead, engineers developed patch for the patch or, in Microsoft's words, "an update that returned the code path to the previously known good state in Windows." The patch was applied to groups of servers and service was gradually restored.

Frame – 31.5" color ePaper display
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
16:23:22 UTC
01:23:22 KST

Introducing Frame
tl;dr
our 3rd release, a full color 31.5" ePaper display in a handmade wooden frame, is now available for pre-order. watch the short film:
the 1st batch is just ~470 units and i intend to ship at least a few by the end of 2026. most deliveries will happen early 2027. see logistics for more details or pre-order here.
background
in 2013 i founded ArtSpot. our vision was to give New Yorkers a bit of joy by exposing them to local art. we did this through informal agreements with dozens of cafes, small galleries, and restaurants. "let us curate art on your walls, get paid if someone buys it."
and it worked. sort of. finding artists was easy, building the platform was easy. getting permission from venues was slow but straightforward. the problem was nobody actually bought the art. i remember the admin email notification that first time a piece was sold. it was a small painting of Janelle Monáe. the buyer was my friend, a gift to me. here it is, still in my possession.
anyway ArtSpot failed. five years later i paid back my investors (+ 13% interest). but the vision never went away. i love making and consuming art.
opinionated platform
i probably say "the most popular feature request since launch is ______" too often. after saying no (and yes) to so many requests, it's tough to keep count.
but with certainty, one of our strongest convictions was about color. TRMNL is not a television. it is not a clock. we avoid trying to do too much.
then grayscale happened. photos look great. art is possible. community member Clark debuted Jaws (yes the movie), 1 frame at a time.
which got us thinking... maybe we were wrong about color. maybe it aligns with our vision and just maybe, it makes it even bigger.
introducing Frame
today i'm thrilled to bury the lede and announce Frame. it's a 31.5 inch full color ePaper display, enclosed in a hand made wooden body that we manufacture ourselves. yes, we opened our own woodworking shop a few miles from HQ. a closer look at the workshop is coming soon.
Frame gets all the same features as other TRMNL devices, with a few additional perks spanning both the web platform and the hardware itself. watch the short film or read along below.
Clock Sync
often requested, always ignored, until now. Frame will update at specified moments of the day versus a relative "every N minutes" cadence. this reduces screen flicker while also extending the battery life and adding continuity to your schedule.
Offline Mode
the internet is cool but totally unnecessary. Frame's microSD port lets you run devices completely offline with zero personal information reaching our servers.
Dedicated Power (optional)
like all TRMNL devices, a rechargeable battery is included (10-20k mAh available). but with Frame we added an extra USB-C port on the rear of the device, accessible with a small hole through the back panel for always-on connectivity.
Color Expertise
some of my colleagues are snobs about ePaper dithering algorithms and LUTs (look-up tables). this is now your gain.
over the past few months we've been developing Lazarus, a color conversion engine that we think provides Frame the best color matching on the market for any Spectra 6 display. it's also coming soon to our 4-color device, and yes it will be open source for your own tuning pleasure.
Three Orientations
Hang Frame in portrait or landscape orientation without additional hardware, both are built-in and flush mounted. You can optionally buy or build your own kickstand.
And More
we're negotiating with some of our favorite community developers to build more Frame-centric features. paying homage to ArtSpot, we just created a Local Art plugin where anyone can submit their work and even sell it through the TRMNL platform.
transparent supply chain
before TRMNL i spent 10 years in b2b software and knew nothing about making physical products for everyday people. nobody ever blasted me on reddit about injection mold flow lines or damaged UPS packages. at best i'd get a G2 review every 3 months.
this all changed in July 2024 and after shipping 60,000 devices to 79 countries we've gotten pickier about operational design. chief among these new requirements is doing as much production as possible in-house.
here are Frame's components and where they're sourced:
by reducing complexity, learning from past releases, and having everything we need either in stock or on order, i expect this to be our smoothest fulfillment cycle yet. as with other devices, all Frames are assembled by our own team and never outsourced.
logistics
Batch #1 is available to customers in locations our USA warehouse already ships to: USA, Canada, Mexico, Australia. pre-order here.
we're open to shipping elsewhere, but Duty / Import fees could be quite high given the product's Customs value. to participate in Batch #1 as a resident outside these countries, go here. this option may be de-activated without notice if inventory sells out.
in early 2027 we plan to open a 2nd woodworking shop near our Berlin, Germany warehouse to offer postage- and Duty-free fulfillment from a TRMNL team near you.

Jolt – Clojure that speaks C
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
16:23:01 UTC
01:23:01 KST

Jolt is a self-hosted Clojure implementation that runs on
        a portable Scheme layer that supports multiple backends.
        Chez natively, Gambit for JavaScript, no JVM. Most Clojure
        runs unchanged, any C library binds natively, and jolt build
        ships a single standalone binary.
      
defcfn turns C functions into ordinary Clojure fnsjolt build emits a single standalone binary with C dependencies linked in staticallyfuture, agent, pmap, and core.async on OS threads
The terminal on the right is jolt itself, compiled to JavaScript by the Gambit backend, evaluating live in your browser. It runs a reduced build to keep the download small, so regex is left out here and says so if you reach for it.
Bind any C shared library: declare it, wrap functions with defcfn, call them with Clojure values. The db library reaches SQLite and Postgres this way; http-client binds OpenSSL and zlib.
jolt build ahead-of-time compiles a project (runtime, standard library, app, and its deps) into a single self-contained executable, with C dependencies linked statically. No Chez, no JVM, no source needed to run it.
Reads Clojure, analyzes it to a host-neutral IR, emits Scheme, and runs it: on Chez natively, or on Gambit compiled to JavaScript. The compiler is written in Clojure and compiles itself; Chez runs interpreted and compiled code identically, so the REPL and a built binary behave the same.
future/promise/agent/pmap run on OS threads over a shared heap, matching JVM semantics. core.async provides channels and go blocks.
Immutable vectors (32-way tries), cons lists, and HAMT maps/sets with Clojure value semantics. Transients are real mutable scratch collections.
Lazy/infinite seqs, transducers, destructuring, multimethods, protocols/records, metadata, namespaces, runtime eval, and the full reader.
Install the self-contained jolt binary: it bundles the runtime, compiler, and standard library, so there's nothing else to install.
# Homebrew
brew install jolt-lang/jolt/jolt
# or the install script (Linux / macOS)
curl -sL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jolt-lang/jolt/main/install | bash
jolt -e '(+ 1 2)'        # => 3
Or run from a clone (needs Chez Scheme); the bootstrap seed is checked in, so there is no build step:
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/jolt-lang/jolt.git
cd jolt
jolt -e '(+ 1 2)'        # => 3$ jolt -e '(->> (range 10) (filter even?) (map (fn [x] (* x x))) (reduce +))'
# 120
$ jolt -e '(/ 1 2)'
# 1/2jolt run -m myapp.core   # resolve deps.edn, then run -main
jolt -M:test [args]      # run an alias's :main-opts
jolt path                # print the resolved source rootsjolt build -m myapp.core -o myapp   # single self-contained executable
./myapp arg1 arg2                        # runs anywhere; args reach -main
# --opt for the optimized build, --dev for an unoptimized one(require '[jolt.ffi :as ffi])
(ffi/load-library "libsqlite3.dylib")  ; or declare :jolt/native in deps.edn
(ffi/defcfn sqlite3-libversion "sqlite3_libversion" [] :string)
(sqlite3-libversion)             ; => "3.51.0"
Any C library binds the same way: the native interop guide covers types, memory, structs, and static linking.
jolt --nrepl-server      # auto-resolves deps.edn, writes .nrepl-port
# connect CIDER / Calva / Cursive via the .nrepl-port file, then
# redefine a var and the next call sees it; no restart
Develop against a live process: see REPL-Driven Development.
Read the documentation for installation, writing libraries, and C interop.
Jolt targets Clojure semantics but runs on Scheme, not the JVM. Most portable Clojure runs unchanged: persistent collections, the numeric tower, lazy seqs, transducers, multimethods, protocols/records, atoms, future/agent/pmap, core.async, runtime eval, and the full reader all behave as on the JVM. Or run from a clone (needs Chez Scheme); the bootstrap seed is checked in, so there is no build step:
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/jolt-lang/jolt.git
cd jolt
jolt -e '(+ 1 2)'        # => 3$ jolt -e '(->> (range 10) (filter even?) (map (fn [x] (* x x))) (reduce +))'
# 120
$ jolt -e '(/ 1 2)'
# 1/2jolt run -m myapp.core   # resolve deps.edn, then run -main
jolt -M:test [args]      # run an alias's :main-opts
jolt path                # print the resolved source rootsjolt build -m myapp.core -o myapp   # single self-contained executable
./myapp arg1 arg2                        # runs anywhere; args reach -main
# --opt for the optimized build, --dev for an unoptimized one(require '[jolt.ffi :as ffi])
(ffi/load-library "libsqlite3.dylib")  ; or declare :jolt/native in deps.edn
(ffi/defcfn sqlite3-libversion "sqlite3_libversion" [] :string)
(sqlite3-libversion)             ; => "3.51.0"
Any C library binds the same way: the native interop guide covers types, memory, structs, and static linking.
jolt --nrepl-server      # auto-resolves deps.edn, writes .nrepl-port
# connect CIDER / Calva / Cursive via the .nrepl-port file, then
# redefine a var and the next call sees it; no restart
Develop against a live process: see REPL-Driven Development.
Read the documentation for installation, writing libraries, and C interop.
Jolt targets Clojure semantics but runs on Scheme, not the JVM. Most portable Clojure runs unchanged: persistent collections, the numeric tower, lazy seqs, transducers, multimethods, protocols/records, atoms, future/agent/pmap, core.async, runtime eval, and the full reader all behave as on the JVM.
