The Secret Thinkpad Powerbutton Code To Bring Dead Laptops Back To Life
Two months ago, I got a new laptop. It’s a Lenovo Thinkpad z61t. I actually ordered a t61, but I accidentally got the z61 instead — and, I actually really like it. It’s quite similar to the t61, but a little smaller and lighter. I was worried that the smaller part would be a problem, but I’ve gotten used to it. I really like the fact that it’s much lighter than my old t42. It just makes it seem so much more usable on the go. Lugging out the t42 was always a chore.
Anyway, I was at the Office 2.0 conference today, where I was giving a little presentation on the Techdirt Insight Community, and about an hour before the presentation, I went to find a quiet place to practice the presentation… and discovered that my brand new laptop wouldn’t work. I knew something was wrong when the “sleep” light wasn’t lit. I started to get worried when I plugged in the laptop and the battery light didn’t light up. Then I noticed that even though the machine had been asleep, it was really really hot. Pushing the power button did nothing. No lights were on and nothing seemed to get them to turn on. I pulled out the battery and put it back in and that did nothing as well.
So I called up IBM support and explained the situation. The guy on the other end then let me in on the secret power button code to revive your dead Thinkpad. After assessing the situation (totally dead laptop) he warned me: “Okay, this is going to sound totally bizarre, but I want you to give this a try…” He then had me unplug the AC adapter and take out the battery. Then, you push the power button 10 times in a row at one second intervals. Next, you push and hold the power button for 30 seconds. Then you put the battery back in and push the power button… and she lives. The computer came back, good as ever.
I asked the guy what the power button pushing incantation did and he said “static discharge” so apparently there was some sort of static that caused a short or something. I tried to get the guy to explain in more detail what happened, but he said “dude, you know as much as I do… but your machine is working.”
And so it is.
So, if you happen to have a Thinkpad that suddenly drops completely dead for no reason, try the power button trick.
Forget up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, B, A. This little code is now the coolest “cheat” code I know…

Jonas on November 2nd, 2011
Hi,
Your trcik worked for me but with something more. As anybody knows now, this problem is caused by residual charge which prevent the Thinkpad to boot (is it a BIOS bug?). The solution is to drain complety the electricity off the Thinkpad and to reboot it.
For me it happened that the button trick wouldn’t work alone. I have to connect my T60 (without the battery) to my unplugged maxi dock, and wait for the “eject” LED to lit. Then I let my Thinkpad as is, the dock’s LED consuming the residual electricity (I let it as is a few hours). When the LED turend OFF, I did the button trick to ensure that no electricity would stay and I replugged the battery. The Thinkpad rebooted, good as new!

RickyJo on March 26th, 2013
I think 2Smart is right. It’s not entirely uncommon for one to have to press the power button once or twice with no power attached to release the residual charge built up in capacitors. When the unit attempts to start it will use up the remaining power in the unsuccessful attempt. From there, you can sometimes start the machine. A common manifestation of this problem is fans spinning but no display. This can manifest after a power outage or other unexpected shut down.
It sounds to me like this particular system board has issues discharging properly.
Having worked phone support myself I know how these sort of myths can spawn and grow–people do what has worked for them without a full understanding of why–which is totally cool most of the time. In the end, it doesn’t matter; regardless of if people press and hold it a few moments or ten times it will still work the same.

WCR on September 10th, 2014
1st off this works on any laptop/model not just think-pad. This isn’t a magic trick, the point of this besides the static discharge, this resets the Bios of computer by pulling all the charge out of the Internal 2032 CMOS Battery, which in return reboots the BIOS. This can happen for many reason not just a static charge, Some computers can have a bad infection that activates when the computer goes to sleep mode, this is a well known attacker, then the virus proceeds to overload your machine to shut down thus causing the bios to have the command programmed to stay shut down. Well by doing the manual BIOS RESET such as this, resets the configurations in the bios back to default.
Also you can try pulling battery out, unplugging charger, and then hold power button for 1 minute if the 10X an 30sec hold doesn’t work for you. And if for some reason it still don’t work, removing the 2032 CMOS Battery on the MOBO for 1 minute or replace it, the battery which is usually located near the RAM on most laptops, not all have the battery located in same place, I suggest if you need to go that far google your model of computer to locate the internal CMOS Battery.
I hope this helps
Wine Computer Repair & Security

I posted in "Who wants to be hired?" and a recruiter sent me a RAT and a stealer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
11:14:27 UTC
20:14:27 KST

A Recruiter Sent Me a Take-Home Test. It Takes Its Orders From an Ethereum Wallet.
A fake recruiter, a VS Code extension that shows one script and runs another, and malware that looks up its server in Ethereum transactions. Read without running a line of it.
On 10 November a recruiter emailed me about a DevOps Engineer role. The email came to the alias from my post in the October “Who wants to be hired?” thread on Hacker News and named two companies from my CV. The next step was a coding assessment inside VS Code, through an extension from the official Marketplace.
I didn’t install it. I downloaded the package, read it, and followed every address it pointed to. At the end of the trail there is a remote-access tool and a credential stealer. The part I enjoyed is in the middle: the malware finds its server by reading the latest transaction of an Ethereum wallet. That wallet is public, so four months of the operator’s server moves, working hours and money are public too.
The email
The message itself was fine: the right role, real employers (both are on my public profile). The problems were one layer down. The sender’s domain, huntrole.org, was registered seven days earlier, the DKIM signature didn’t verify, and iCloud had already filed the message as spam. And the assessment could only be done in an extension that starts together with the editor.
The careers site won’t take an application without a PDF resume, so it collects CVs even from people who never open VS Code. I sent it an invented candidate and got a ticket ID and instructions pointing at the extension.
The extension shows one script and runs another
There is no malware in the package, and that’s the design. On every editor start the extension (huntrole.assessment-tool, 126 installs on 16 November) sends the hostname and VS Code’s machineId to api.huntrole.com and keeps a WebSocket open.
When the assessment panel opens, the server returns a task with two code fields. The panel “types” displayScript on screen, then passes script to new Function with the real require and process: files, network, child processes. No ticket and no Run button needed.
For a device the server didn’t know, script was 150 harmless bytes. After my invented device registered and opened the socket it was 8,665 bytes, and displayScript hadn’t changed. So a scanner sees a clean package, and so does a candidate who reads the files before installing.
The server address is a transaction
The long script has no server address in it. It has a wallet address and code that looks up the wallet’s latest transaction. With the names cleaned up:
const wallet = "0x1eEf0849EDa15d87f64e51C73C8442Cf3c8bCEF3".toLowerCase();
function decode(to) {
  const bytes = Buffer.from(to.replace(/^0x/i, ""), "hex");
  const ip = (b) => b[0] + "." + b[1] + "." + b[2] + "." + b[3];
  return [ip(bytes.subarray(0, 4)), ip(bytes.subarray(4, 8))];
}
to is the recipient of that transaction. An Ethereum address is 20 bytes, and the operator fills them with an IPv4 address, the same address again, and 12 bytes that spell helloipbot!!. The transaction moves zero ETH and nobody owns the recipient.
From here on, that recipient is a marker, a transaction to it is a ping, and the sender is a pointer wallet.
The script doesn’t search for the ping. It rounds the current block number down to a multiple of 1,000 and opens six blocks around the round numbers, so the writer has to be punctual. If those are empty it falls back to a block explorer, and nothing checks the record’s age, so a wallet that has stopped writing still points at its last server.
For the operator this is cheap and hard to take down: no registrar can remove the pointer, and a ping costs about 0.00007 ETH. In exchange, every server they ever used, and the minute they switched to it, stays on a public ledger for good.
Three wallets, eleven servers
Every marker ends in the same 12 bytes, so the wallets can be found from the other side. I scanned every Ethereum transaction since 1 April for that ending and got three senders. Between them: 1,157 pings to 11 servers from July to 15 November.
- The early wallet worked for three weeks in July and starts with a developer’s test transactions: the text hello as data, markers that decode to addresses no packet can reach. I couldn’t find it in any public report.
- The second ran from 25 July to 19 October, with 607 pings to eight servers. It’s the wallet from the August reports on trojanised npm packages.
- The third is the one in my script: 303 pings to five servers since 4 September. It last switched on 12 November, two days after the email.
Nine of the eleven servers, and api.huntrole.com too, sit at one hosting company, Evoxt. The two newest are at another, Virtuo, side by side in one /24.
The timer counts blocks
The typical gap between pings is 200.6 minutes, which is exactly 1,000 blocks. Of the third wallet’s 303 pings, 270 landed in a block whose number ends in 999, 000 or 001, the blocks the script opens first. The timer keeps a fresh copy of the record where the reader will look, even when the address hasn’t changed.
The treasury that pays for this keeps hours. Its key has signed 284 transactions on 14 chains over 37 days, none of them between 12:00 and 22:59 UTC. The email’s Date header says +0500, and on that clock the signing hours look like a working day. Both are trivial to fake, so I won’t name a time zone.
Where the gas money comes from
The pointer wallets have burned about 0.08 ETH in four months. One treasury wallet funded two of the three, and each of its three top-ups was followed by a server change: 7 minutes, 8 minutes and 44 hours later.
The treasury’s own money looks stolen, though the ledger alone can’t prove it. On 3 September nine wallets, idle for months and mostly tied to each other by old transfers, sent it what they held within half an hour, on Ethereum and several other chains. The treasury sold the tokens, bridged about 12,560 USDC to BNB Chain and cashed out through one-time addresses of what looks like a swap service. Nine days later someone, I think the owner, moved what was left to a fresh address, and none of it went to the treasury.
It happened again on 3 November. A private wallet sent the treasury 5,344 USDT on BNB Chain and a little ETH on Ethereum within four minutes, and about twenty minutes later the treasury swapped it and moved it on.
Wallet files are on the stealer’s list, but nothing on chain says it emptied these wallets. Their addresses stay out of this post.
The treasury also pays people: 32 USDT transfers to eight addresses since September, 3,813 USDT in total, at most 21% of what those addresses received this year. Two of the eight cash out through an address that forwards everything to a wallet the block explorer labels OKX, and two more into one labelled Lemon Cash. Both exchanges verify their customers. If the labels are right, someone with the authority to ask can get names.
Going in, there is no such door: two of the pointer wallets got their first ETH from FixedFloat, an exchange that asks for no identity.
The same wallets feed npm and PyPI
The recruiter front is one delivery channel of several. The second wallet’s address is quoted in at least 40 advisories in the OpenSSF malicious-packages repository, nearly all for npm. On 9 November JFrog described another fake recruiting company, AccuraSoftHire, whose take-home project reads the same wallet through the same paths with the same XOR keys. And the October reports on hijacked npm packages from GitGuardian, OX Security and Sonatype name the third wallet, the one in my script.
What arrives on the machine
I fetched each stage once from a disposable VM and decoded it without executing anything: two small loaders, a remote-access tool, a 1.4 MB injector that plants code into other applications, and a Python stealer.
The remote-access tool is byte-identical to a published DEV#POPPER sample. It dials out, so a home router doesn’t stop it, and it accepts arbitrary shell commands. The stealer copies browser databases, keychain files and wallet files. Since I ran nothing, I can’t say what it actually gets from a real machine. The injector I mostly couldn’t read.
Who is behind it
Vendor reports on related incidents attribute this family (PolinRider, DEV#POPPER) to North Korean groups. My data ties HuntRole to the family through identical bytes, shared wallets and shared servers. It says nothing about the country.
Is this the crew that took about 6.3 billion dollars from Binance on 29 October? By Binance’s account that attack also went through a fake hiring process with a coding assignment. None of the 453 addresses around this ledger is among the 608 Ethereum addresses in the FBI alert, and Binance has published no hashes or servers to compare. I found no link and can’t rule one out.
If you installed it
Check for the extension and for what the remote-access tool leaves behind:
code --list-extensions | grep -i huntrolels -la ~/.node_modules/ 2>/dev/null | grep -i npm-wsfind ~ /Applications \( -name "*.inz.cjs" -o -name "*.inz.orig" -o -name "*.inz.tmp" \) 2>/dev/null
- Installed, panel never opened. The server has your hostname and machine ID. As far as the code shows, nothing else ran. The extension can open the panel on its own, though, so if in doubt count it as opened.
- Panel opened. Assume the script ran, whatever the checks show.
- Any of those files exist. The machine is compromised. From another device, rotate everything your account could read: .env files, browser passwords and sessions, Git and cloud credentials, wallet seeds. Then reinstall Node and the patched applications, or rebuild the machine.
When Microsoft removes a malicious extension, VS Code uninstalls it automatically (so its documentation says). Whatever the tool planted stays.
Who has been told
On 15 November I reported the extension to Microsoft, the domains and mailbox to Namecheap, the careers site to Vercel, and the servers to Evoxt and Virtuo. Two hours later I had automatic acknowledgements. A day later the extension is still listed.
The operator was busy that day too. Five hours before my reports the treasury signed 29 transactions on ten chains, most of them moving its leftovers to an address it had never used. The next morning that address signed for the first time: it swapped some BNB into USDT and sent 60 USDT to one of the eight addresses the old treasury had been paying. It pays the same people, so I’m calling it the new treasury.
How I read it without running it
Coding agents did most of the reading, and a sample can talk to the model that reads it: a planted AGENTS.md is a prompt injection attempt. So the sample was only ever data, the model reading it had no network, no shell and no secrets, and anything dynamic ran in a disposable microVM with the network closed by default.
Indicators

Doing Show HN generates a ton of automated email pitches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
11:00:02 UTC
20:00:02 KST

Show HN -> a ton of automated email pitches
I posted Airdash on Show HN last week. Over the next four days, 17 services wrote to the Airdash inbox to sell me something, and nearly all of them were written by software that read my HN title and nothing else.
Let's go through it.
Seven of the 17 are launch boards and directories: AI tool lists, "Product of the Week" battles, a 3D city map of SaaS products. The hook is usually a dofollow backlink, the price somewhere between free and $49. The other ten sell security scans, competitor reports, agent testing, demo videos, Reddit promotion, newsletter sponsorships, distribution to other people's coding agents, and one wants an affiliate deal.
"SQLite databases for agents with an Airtable view" shows up in almost every email, reworded just enough to look like someone read it. One directory pasted my whole Show HN title in as the product name, so it would love to feature "I built SQLite databases for your agents with an Airtable view for you."
"No follow-ups, promise." "This is the only email you'll get about it." "Not a mailing list, just a one-time note." One of them then sent me the same pitch three times.
Here they are in order of arrival, Madrid time. I replaced the names of the services and the people with [brackets] and took out the links, to protect the innocent.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Show HN -> a ton of automated email pitches
I posted Airdash on Show HN last week. Over the next four days, 17 services wrote to the Airdash inbox to sell me something, and nearly all of them were written by software that read my HN title and nothing else.
Let's go through it.
Seven of the 17 are launch boards and directories: AI tool lists, "Product of the Week" battles, a 3D city map of SaaS products. The hook is usually a dofollow backlink, the price somewhere between free and $49. The other ten sell security scans, competitor reports, agent testing, demo videos, Reddit promotion, newsletter sponsorships, distribution to other people's coding agents, and one wants an affiliate deal.
"SQLite databases for agents with an Airtable view" shows up in almost every email, reworded just enough to look like someone read it. One directory pasted my whole Show HN title in as the product name, so it would love to feature "I built SQLite databases for your agents with an Airtable view for you."
"No follow-ups, promise." "This is the only email you'll get about it." "Not a mailing list, just a one-time note." One of them then sent me the same pitch three times.

Senator slams Commerce Secretary for flow of Nvidia AI chips to China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
10:52:52 UTC
19:52:52 KST

Washington Sen. Maria Cantwell, one of the top Democrats on the Senate commerce committee, has taken fire at the Department of Commerce (DOC) under Secretary Howard Lutnick for neglecting to enforce protections intended to keep Nvidia’s AI chips away from China. In a letter to Lutnick on Sunday, Cantwell said the DOC has “undermined America’s national security” and that its failures “help give away America’s technology advantage in AI.”
Senator slams commerce secretary for flow of Nvidia AI chips to China
Amid the Jensen Huang fallout, Maria Cantwell accuses Howard Lutnick of giving away ‘America’s technology advantage in AI.’
“Despite clear authority from Congress, the Department of Commerce has allowed advanced AI chips to flow through companies with ties to the People’s Republic of China (PRC). The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology.”
In her letter, Cantwell specifically calls out instances when the DOC reportedly didn’t heed warnings from White House and intelligence officials to restrict Megaspeed’s access to AI chips, prior to allegations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a then-Megaspeed executive suspected of being a Chinese spy. Cantwell also criticizes the DOC for allowing Alibaba and ByteDance to access Nvidia chips through overseas data centers, and extending a loophole that let restricted companies obtain American AI technology through subsidiaries.
The DOC is also accused of “putting business interests ahead of national security,” with Cantwell noting that Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services firm formerly led by Lutnick and now steered by his sons, reportedly held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of Lutnick’s nomination for commerce secretary.
The letter comes ahead of a meeting in China this Thursday between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. While Congress is looking to bolster export restrictions around AI chips, The Wall Street Journal reports that Lutnick is instead expected to unveil a new initiative that will designate Nvidia — along with companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon, and Microsoft — as an AI “national champion.” The designation reportedly aims to help these companies expand overseas and compete with Chinese technology firms by granting them expedited export licence approvals.
“America cannot maintain its leadership in AI if the agency responsible for protecting that advantage fails to enforce its own controls,” Cantwell said, closing her letter. “The Administration must account for its failure to enforce these protections and take immediate action to prevent America’s most sensitive technology from strengthening our adversaries.”

It's always DNS, so why are we running our own?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
09:19:38 UTC
18:19:38 KST

This will be a rollercoaster story on how we ended up replacing Route53 and running our own authoritative DNS server.
Before our lives changed
At some point, we decided we should be able to provide unlimited basins to our clients. Basins are a core namespace construct on S2 and act as top-level containers for streams (already unlimited in number). We found that customers were hacking around our not-so-arbitrary limit of 100 basins per account. That’s not a cool experience.
For the purposes of this story, what is important is that each basin created by a customer becomes its own subdomain: my-basin.b.s2.dev (not different from the way buckets work on AWS S3). The DNS entry associated with each basin is a CNAME, which routes clients to the correct cell in our architecture. To support unlimited basins, we'd therefore need to support unlimited DNS records.
These records would need strong consistency too. When a basin is created, its address should be instantly resolvable, otherwise clients would be waiting around for a cached NXDOMAIN to expire.
My pulse went through the roof at the thought of running our own DNS server, yikes!
Hooking on existing systems
My research phase started with hope. Hope that our existing DNS setup with AWS Route53 would work with these new requirements. I really really did not want us to build and run our own DNS server.
Route53 is an awesome system and can, it appears, support an unlimited number of records. But, there's a fatal limitation: their API rate limits at a max of about 5 UPSERTs per second (AWS throttling docs have recently changed, the limits may be higher now).
This was something we discovered the hard way, actually. I did read the docs but the API limits didn’t raise any concerns. It became obvious when a nefarious actor rapidly created 10s of thousands of basins, saturating our entire quota of Route53 records. This generated a backlog of work that required a few hours to process, during which our normal DNS updates were stuck, with processes trying to delete records while others tried to add new records. It did make for a great post-incident review though. This was when we started enforcing the 100 basins per account limit.
We looked at the option of batching, but that would break our goal of making entries instantly available. And even with batching, the setup did not feel “unlimited”; it would still be possible for legitimate use of the system to hit the rate limit.
Other managed DNS providers we looked at (GCP Cloud DNS, Cloudflare, Azure DNS) have similar limitations: if you update/insert/upsert records using the provider API, there’s a heavy limiting component.
No way around it, a custom authoritative DNS server had to be built (double yikes!)
The new DNS system
The technical requirements were pretty straightforward: given any DNS request that comes in, we need to query an up-to-date zone map, which should be able to hold unlimited records, and send a corresponding response back to the client.
To avoid syncing to a separate system and having yet another moving piece, the DNS records would come directly from our existing basin database. A live SELECT would consistently “resolve” the required mapping in the DNS request. In other words, we wanted DNS to simply become a new caller of our existing, strongly consistent account database.
Our account database lives in Google’s Cloud Spanner where performance was expected to fare well (given enough money that is).
Next came the core functionality.
We went back and forth between building on a library or writing a CoreDNS module. A library ended up feeling like the most flexible path, which would allow us to build something very specific to our use case. We are a Rust shop, but we decided to go with Go for this project, mostly because the Spanner tooling (and the GCP ecosystem) is comparatively more mature. We quickly settled on the miekg/dns library due to its excellent doc quality and the many RFCs under its belt.
We needed to be able to support authoritative DNS queries for several types of records: A, AAAA, NS, CNAME, SOA. Since we were using a library we had to build the responses ourselves. Our correctness testing focused on these, and consisted of unit tests, RFC compliance testing using Ferret (which we discovered in this great paper: SCALE: Automatically Finding RFC Compliance Bugs in DNS Nameservers) and a post-deploy smoke test with live data.
S2 uses wildcard certificates for the basin zone and they need ACME DNS-01 challenges to work. We decided not to serve the DNS challenge from our server and offloaded it to a separate Route53 zone using CNAME delegation, to avoid tweaking our cert renewal systems as well as serving dynamic TXT records.
We then went through a few planning sessions with a popular AI system. The design was simple enough, things made a lot of sense (even for me), except that the recommendations constantly included various extra features: coalescing, negative caching, throttling, rate limiting, DNS cookies, etc. Expected, for a system that would sit live on the open scary internet; however, it was a lot of suggested protection.
The more we pulled on this thread ... the scarier it got. There are many types of attacks that can happen at the DNS level, scary things I knew of and things I never heard of.
NXDOMAIN attack is the one that made us the most afraid. Every random non-existent DNS query would be a fresh database lookup. We tried building in-app defenses for NXDOMAIN however, it is, in my opinion, the worst DDoS attack and nothing can really stop it. Not cool.
The case for a DNS Firewall
Long story short, the possible attacks on DNS infrastructure scared me more than I would like to admit. We went looking for a DNS firewall solution. We were sure there must be something like a reverse proxy setup for DNS serving. Either this is a niche setup or it’s a very dangerous world, but for our requirements of unlimited records and DNS reverse-proxy firewall type, we found only two companies: Cloudflare and Akamai. Both giants in their own rights, both with similar offerings (it’s the kind that has no public pricing).
A few POCs later, we ended up picking Cloudflares DNS Firewall solution. Our DNS server origins were configured to only allow traffic from Cloudflare’s known IPs, a pretty standard reverse-CF setup (Cloudflare in front and nobody else gets to the origin, otherwise what’s the point). With this missing piece, we were now at our final design and ready to roll the new system into production.
As an authoritative DNS server, we have to reply to SOA and NS queries, and they point to nameserver IPs. We took extra care to ensure the IPs returned are always the Cloudflare IPs and not the load balancer ones, which included a ns-leak-test that ensures the origin IPs don't leak as part of some regression change.
Final architecture
For the final architecture and HA (yes, failures will always happen), we run the DNS server on two separate GKE clusters (in separate regions, choosing the closest possible to Spanner), each with multiple replicas behind a TCP and UDP load balancer.
Observability and training everyone on the new system were another key component of the rollout. While I don’t think anyone gives Route53 a second thought and I don’t think anyone monitors it separately (managed services are someone else’s pager after all), we had to create alerts and runbooks with late-night processes to recover from failures.
There is one funny part to this setup: explaining the full delegation chain. The main domain is managed by Cloudflare in a regular zone. Then it delegates the basin subdomain to Cloudflare, but not a zone, to a service (DNS Firewall). That service then connects to GKE. And there’s another zone in Route53 for the certs (good luck understanding that, Codex).
This isn’t even its final form, the internal TODO includes tuning DNS caching and how to properly optimize between clients/DNS Firewall/DNS app (no amount of AI can solve that), future DNSSEC extensions and many more. It is an unknown system when it comes to failures we don’t see (or the way I like to think about this, how do you know things fail when they look fine).
For now, things have been stable. Looking at stats for the past few weeks, live traffic looks good, the commit history for the past few weeks is mostly CVE fixes, dependency bumps and cost savings. Our customers now create thousands of basins, and they are instantly available for streaming.
I think we’re now in a place where we can blame DNS in one of our post-incident reviews.

It's always DNS, so why are we running our own?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
09:19:38 UTC
18:19:38 KST

This will be a rollercoaster story on how we ended up replacing Route53 and running our own authoritative DNS server.
Before our lives changed
At some point, we decided we should be able to provide unlimited basins to our clients. Basins are a core namespace construct on S2 and act as top-level containers for streams (already unlimited in number). We found that customers were hacking around our not-so-arbitrary limit of 100 basins per account. That’s not a cool experience.
For the purposes of this story, what is important is that each basin created by a customer becomes its own subdomain: my-basin.b.s2.dev (not different from the way buckets work on AWS S3). The DNS entry associated with each basin is a CNAME, which routes clients to the correct cell in our architecture. To support unlimited basins, we'd therefore need to support unlimited DNS records.
These records would need strong consistency too. When a basin is created, its address should be instantly resolvable, otherwise clients would be waiting around for a cached NXDOMAIN to expire.
My pulse went through the roof at the thought of running our own DNS server, yikes!
Hooking on existing systems
My research phase started with hope. Hope that our existing DNS setup with AWS Route53 would work with these new requirements. I really really did not want us to build and run our own DNS server.
Route53 is an awesome system and can, it appears, support an unlimited number of records. But, there's a fatal limitation: their API rate limits at a max of about 5 UPSERTs per second (AWS throttling docs have recently changed, the limits may be higher now).
This was something we discovered the hard way, actually. I did read the docs but the API limits didn’t raise any concerns. It became obvious when a nefarious actor rapidly created 10s of thousands of basins, saturating our entire quota of Route53 records. This generated a backlog of work that required a few hours to process, during which our normal DNS updates were stuck, with processes trying to delete records while others tried to add new records. It did make for a great post-incident review though. This was when we started enforcing the 100 basins per account limit.
We looked at the option of batching, but that would break our goal of making entries instantly available. And even with batching, the setup did not feel “unlimited”; it would still be possible for legitimate use of the system to hit the rate limit.

Purism Announces 'Librem 5 v2' Linux Phone with RISC-V SoC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

08:34:00 UTC
17:34:00 KST

Purism Announces 'Librem 5 v2' Linux Phone with RISC-V SoC (omgubuntu.co.uk) 41
			
		 	
				From the Linux-news blog OMG Ubuntu:
Purism is crowdfunding a new version of its  Librem 5 Linux smartphone, this one powered by RISC-V rather than Arm. 
Librem 5 v2 will use an octa-core SpacemiT K1 RISC-V SoC, replacing the quad-core Arm64 NXP CPU.  This processor shift will provide better performance and longer battery life than the original Librem 5 and not run as hot in use.  Memory is bumped to 8 GB RAM, up from 3 GB, and storage leaps to 128 GB from 32 GB. Librem 5 v2 will run PureOS, Purism's Debian-based operating system using Phosh as its UI.   SD card read speeds are faster, which is handy since the device can boot a second OS from a memory card. On-board hardware encoding means the Librem 5 will be able to take 13 megapixel photos and shoot high-definition video for the first time....
"RISC-V is the future, and Librem 5 v2 is the perfect product to bring it to a mainstream audience", Jonathon Hall, CTO at Purism, says of the launch.
"Freeing us from the control of Big Tech starts with the foundation, and RISC-V's foundation frees us from the oligarchy. The Librem 5 v2 puts you in control of your data, combining that with the ease of use we expect in the modern era".
 
Its specifications include a 5.7-inch 720 x 1440 display, hardware kill switches, and a removable 4500mAh battery, writes Slashdot reader BrianFagioli:
The asking price is $1,599, with production delivery targeted for roughly May 2028.. Purism acknowledges remaining work on graphics, peripheral drivers, ARM64 app emulation, and power management.  NERDS.xyz argues that the concept is appealing, but the price and wait are difficult to justify for an everyday phone. Android already uses the Linux kernel, so the appeal here is an alternative built around PureOS and the broader desktop Linux ecosystem. Is this a reasonable cost to help fund that alternative, or too much money for hardware and software that buyers cannot yet evaluate as a finished product?  
Purism says they've already received 53 of their goal of 2,500 orders (2%) with 91 days still remaining. (The campaign runs through February 15 of 2027)

Winudf – DVD / BluRay driver for DOS, Windows 1.x – 3x / 95 / 98 / ME
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
08:00:13 UTC
17:00:13 KST

WINUDF reads and writes UDF (versions 1.02 to 2.60), the file system of DVDs, Blu-ray
discs, packet-written CDs and UDF-formatted USB sticks and disks: WINUDF.EXE gives DOS and
Windows 1.0x–3.11 drive letters for them, WINUDF.VXD is a file system driver for Windows
95 / 98 / ME with long names.
WINUDF is one of the four WINDRV packages, each in its own repository and usable alone or together with the others:
From DOS (or an MS-DOS box of Windows 95 / 98 / ME), in bin\DOS of this package:
INSTUDF                      default directory, AUTOEXEC.BAT / SYSTEM.INI updated
INSTUDF C:\DRV /O /L:R       another directory; options for WINUDF.EXE after /O (letters from R:)
DOS / Windows 3.x: WINUDF.EXE goes to AUTOEXEC.BAT after MSCDEX, LASTDRIVE=Z to
CONFIG.SYS when needed. Windows 95 / 98 / ME: WINUDF.VXD goes to WINDOWS\SYSTEM and
device=WINUDF.VXD to [386Enh] of SYSTEM.INI. The originals are saved as *.WNF.
Uninstall: UNINUDF.
- DOS and Windows 1.0x–3.11: LASTDRIVE=Z in CONFIG.SYS, and in AUTOEXEC.BAT after the
MSCDEX line: C:\WINDRV\WINUDF.EXE
- Windows 95 / 98 / ME: copy bin\WIN9X\WINUDF.VXD to C:\WINDOWS\SYSTEM and add device=WINUDF.VXD to the [386Enh] section of SYSTEM.INI.
bin/DOS     DOS: the driver, its 32-bit core, tools, installer and uninstaller (also all
            Windows 1.0x / 2.x need)
bin/WIN3X   Windows 3.0, 3.1 and Windows for Workgroups 3.11
bin/WIN9X   Windows 95, 98 and ME (Plug and Play drivers and their INF files: the folder
            to give to "Have Disk" / "Update Driver")
src         the source code (see "Building")
Files used by several systems are in each of their folders. The installer is run from
bin\DOS; it takes the files of the other systems from the folders next to it, so the
bin tree has to stay together (copy all of it to a floppy or a directory).
MANUAL.md (MANUAL.TXT in bin\DOS, WINUDF.TXT for Windows) describes everything
else: all options, how the driver works, hardware and chipset notes, the programming
interface, building from source, tests and known limitations.
1.2 (2 November 2026)
Changelog:
- Program Manager (Windows 3.x): an Uninstall WINUDF item with a red cross on the disk icon (Windows closes, UNINUDF /REBOOT runs and restarts the computer). The banner lists the systems (DOS, Windows 1.x/2.x/3.x/95/98/ME).
- Windows 95/98/ME: programs on UDF discs (and WINUDF's own installer) no longer crash with 0xC0000005. The buffer of a read or write is locked before the driver starts: a page of the program's own image could be paged in from the same disc in the middle of the request, and the page-in then used the driver's block cache and transfer buffer, so the program got the data of the page-in.
- Extents of files written or filled are never longer than an extent can describe (just under 1 GB): a hole filled at once was one extent of any size (and its length overflowed into the type bits); merging blocks into the last extent can no longer overflow either.
- DOS: buffers are normalized before device transfers, so a 32 KB transfer never runs past the end of a 64 KB segment.
- Long file names: INT 21h 716Ch passes the caller's mode, attributes and action to DOS as they are (the create action was masked off); on DOS 3.x, which has no function 6Ch, the file is opened with function 3Dh (issues #9, #12).
- INT 21h 7142h accepts negative positions, like DOS's own seek (issue #11).
- The high dword of a file position beyond 4 GB is kept in the file's system file table entry (offset 07h, free for a redirector) instead of a table of eight entries: any number of open files can be beyond 4 GB (issue #10).
- Before staying resident, handles 0-19 are closed without looking at the job file table (issue #8).
- Unloading follows interrupt handlers whose IISP header has a jump of any kind before the 'KB' signature (issue #7).
- The texts of WINUDF.EXE, the VxD and the documentation name Windows 1.0 to ME.
1.1 (26 October 2026)
Changelog:
- Added long file names in DOS: WINUDF.EXE answers the long file name API of MS-DOS 7 (INT 21h AX=71xxh: find first / next, open / create, attributes, rename, delete, directories, short / long name, file times), so DIR, COPY and other programs of MS-DOS 7.x show and use the long names of UDF disks; free space (7303h) and 64-bit file positions (7142h) for files of 4 GB and more.
- WINUDF.EXE is a regular DOS program that can be loaded high (LH), about 70 KB resident; its interrupt handlers follow the IBM interrupt sharing protocol, so it unloads (/U) after other TSRs that hooked the same interrupts.
- Works next to SHSUCDX (UDF DVDs of SHSUCDX's drives) and MSCDEX.
- Fixed unloading and the "already loaded" check.
- Fixed Windows 98 freezing on UDF disks in partitions Windows 9x calls unformatted (they are read through the BIOS path now).
- Fixed the "disk structure is corrupted" error when copying folders to UDF disks in Windows 98.
- Fixed WritePrivateProfileString (INI files) and Explorer writing desktop.ini hanging on UDF drives in Windows 95/98/ME: WINUDF.VXD answers the drive IOCTLs (removable, remote, drive map) itself.
- Added writing to Windows 10 UDF 2.60 disks (metadata bitmap embedded in its file entry).
- The volume is written and closed when the disk is removed safely.
- Added MS-DOS 7.0, 7.1, 8.0 and FreeDOS support; the installer puts WINUDF.EXE into AUTOEXEC.BAT there too (only Windows 95/98/ME use DOSSTART.BAT).
- The documentation is split into README.md (overview, installation) and MANUAL.md (all details).
1.0 (12 October 2026) — first release: UDF 1.02–2.60 read / write, WINUDF.EXE for DOS
and Windows 1.0x–3.11, WINUDF.VXD for Windows 95 / 98 / ME.
1.0 update (14 October 2026): the package is split into bin/DOS, bin/WIN3X and
bin/WIN9X; English documentation.

How Should Armies Fight?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
07:57:40 UTC
16:57:40 KST

A review of The Arms of the Future by Jack Watling.
Occasionally a book gets the next war right. In 1937, Heinz Guderian argued in Achtung – Panzer! that tanks should concentrate in armored formations, that those formations were best controlled by radio, and that their purpose was to break through enemy lines and fight beyond them. In 1940, Guderian used a German tank corps to punch through French defenses and trap almost two million Allied soldiers.
Jack Watling may have written another book like that. Watling, a British military analyst who works closely with the Ukrainian general staff, published The Arms of the Future in 2023. It argues that three forces define war today: the reach of sensors, the range of weapons, and the precision of munitions. All three are improving and have made the way armies previously fought impossible.
Sensors come in many forms. They include cameras mounted on consumer drones, commercial satellites and ground surveillance radars. Some listen: an acoustic sensor carried by a single soldier can identify a tank from ten kilometers away. Others use lasers to detect heartbeats or electronic emissions to locate a soldier making a phone call.
Once the sensors have found a target, modern munitions can destroy it from much further away. Eighty years ago, heavy artillery firing at sixteen kilometers missed by an average of fifty meters. In tests today, heavy artillery firing at seventy kilometers misses by an average of just two meters. Other weapons like rocket artillery and kamikaze drones regularly hit targets at twice that range.
This is a problem for the way modern militaries, including Western ones, fight. Generals try to combine surprise and concentration: secretly assembling a large group of soldiers and tanks and quickly overpowering the enemy. But both are impossible if a radar operator can spot vehicles assembling from fifty kilometers away and artillerymen start hitting them minutes later.
Already, grouping vehicles in Ukraine within a few tens of kilometers of the front line often gets them destroyed. As sensors and munitions improve, this ‘gray zone’ keeps growing, reaching far into what used to be the rear. The countryside, traditionally the place where generals like to maneuver, has become extremely dangerous: any concentration of forces is detected and then destroyed from a distance. How, then, should armies fight?
The first option soldiers have is to make themselves not worth shooting. They can do this by dispersing and hardening – digging deep holes and sitting in them. This is a great tactic when defending, but ensures that any attack they mount will be piecemeal and bloody.
Their second option is to withdraw to the places where cameras cannot see them and shells struggle to kill them: cities. To the modern soldier, the urban environment is like a warren of tunnels, full of shelters that preserve mobility. They require specialized troops to attack, and even then, fighting is difficult. But an army that ignores the countryside will soon find itself surrounded and cut off, and sitting in a city doesn’t solve the problem of attacking the enemy.
Their third option, and Watling’s preference, is to try to restore movement and surprise by fighting the sensors themselves. The ideal army of the future combines small groups of highly mobile soldiers that target enemy sensors and deploy their own with heavy artillery that support them from further back and specialized assault units that fight over cities and other strongpoints. The hope is not to revive the long offensives of Guderian’s tanks but to create a brief window in which troops can assemble and take a single objective without being spotted and destroyed.
The Arms of the Future came out three years ago, and Ukraine is still the site of a major ground war. Since then, that war has evolved along the lines Watling predicted. Most Ukrainian soldiers live underground, sometimes for months at a time and hundreds of meters from the nearest friendly unit. They avoid movement whenever possible and, when forced to hold ground, prefer towns and cities, as they did at Pokrovsk and Kostyantynivka. A Ukrainian battalion commander tells Watling: ‘I don’t need reinforcements, I need buildings to fight from.’ The attacking Russians, who have no holes to sit in, no cities to shelter in, and can neither concentrate nor achieve surprise, are suffering astonishing losses.
That doesn't mean successful attacks have become entirely impossible. Some Ukrainian units, like the Third Assault Brigade, are learning to fight as Watling would want, targeting enemy sensors before grouping together and rushing forward. These attacks appear to be working, and may keep the battlefield moving for a while. But they will succeed only as long as they manage to keep blinding the enemy. If the cameras keep improving and the shells keep flying, that too may stop being an option.

“…and the proof is checked in Lean”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
07:38:19 UTC
16:38:19 KST

This post is an attempt to explain in simple terms how to interpret claims of the form “this theorem is correct because it was checked in Lean”. The summary is: there is an important signal that can be extracted from Lean code, but if this code is AI-generated then you need to do some tests first. We explain the tests, and note that in many cases (such as the OpenAI theorem dump) these tests have not yet been systematically done.
Introduction
Last month’s theorem dump by OpenAI consisted of 722 mathematics papers, around 45% of which came with some Lean code. Three of the (non-Leanified) papers have since been retracted because of a sign error. Some people might say “well, the papers that come with Lean code are definitely correct because that’s how Lean works”. Others might say “well Lean had a soundness bug and could well have more, and AIs will reward hack, so Lean verification doesn’t tell us much at all”. The truth, unsurprisingly, is more subtle, and this post is an attempt to explain it.
This post is structured as a sequence of four questions that one needs to ask about a Lean repository, particularly if it is AI-generated, before one can start to make correctness claims of this form. And before I start, let me stress that for many of the papers in the OpenAI theorem dump, these questions have not yet all been answered affirmatively (but there is nothing stopping people from answering these questions, and I have no reason to believe that any of the tests below will fail, it’s just that people didn’t do them yet).
Question 1. Does the Lean statement match the informal statement?
A Lean repository will typically have a “headline theorem statement”. This will be some computer code which defines the statement (not the proof!) of a theorem. Note the huge difference here between the statement, and the proof. For example here is some fully-compiling Lean code which defines a mathematical statement.
import Mathlibdef FermatsLastTheorem : Prop :=   ∀ a b c n : ℕ, n ≥ 3 → a^n + b^n ≠ c^n 
		
This code imports Lean’s mathematics library Mathlib and then defines a mathematical statement which looks at first glance like it might be Fermat’s Last Theorem, but which actually is a trivially false statement because in Lean ℕ contains 0, so a = b = c = 0 and n = 3 gives a counterexample. This does not stop the statement from compiling! It will however stop any proof of this statement from compiling. Lean carefully distinguishes between the statement of a theorem and the proof of a theorem; humans are very good at referring to both ideas as “a theorem”.
The first question which one has to ask when judging a pdf which comes with some Lean code is: “what is the statement of the theorem in the Lean code, and does this correspond to the actual theorem statement in the pdf?” For a human Lean expert, this is typically (but not always) an easy question to answer. For example any Lean-competent human mathematician would be able to read the two lines of code above and observe that this was a mis-statement of Fermat’s Last Theorem.
Things are, however, not always as easy as this. Currently, because of deficiencies in available libraries, one may have to read many thousands of lines of code just to understand the statement of a formalised theorem. An example of this right now is a PR to DeepMind’s Formal Conjectures repository containing a Lean formalisation of the statement of the Hodge conjecture. At the time of writing, the statement relies on over 10,000 lines of code sitting on top of Mathlib, because Mathlib (which is carefully human-expert-checked and which can be trusted) does not yet have the definitions of things like the cycle class map needed to make the statement. Another example is Axiom’s recent announcement of a formally-verified proof of the classification of finite simple groups. The statement which Axiom’s system proved is here in Tau Ceti, an AI-generated library of Lean code. The file containing the statement imports over 250K lines of Lean code in Tau Ceti (over 900 files). Of these, around 5600 lines of code are crucial because they contain all the relevant definitions (for example, all the definitions of the sporadic simple groups, most of which are still not in Mathlib). Without human checking, one does not really know for sure that this is definitely the correct statement of the classification (and note that I have not yet met any human who claims to have carefully checked that the definitions of the sporadic groups in Tau Ceti are correct). In fact by far the strongest evidence that we have that this statement is correctly formalized is that Axiom’s code proves it!
It is worth noting that of the 290 OpenAI theorems which come with Lean code, around 38 of them have the property that the Lean code does not even state, let alone prove, the main theorem of the paper. And OpenAI never claimed that it did! They just said “here is some Lean code which goes with this paper”. Sometimes the code just states and proves some intermediate results — my impression is that OpenAI decided to go live when some of the formalizations were incomplete, so just dumped what they had. To give a concrete example: paper 194 claims to prove Lech’s multiplicity conjecture in commutative algebra, with no restriction on dimension, residue field or characteristic; this question has been open since 1960. The headline theorem in the corresponding Lean code can be checked to be Corollary 5.4 of the paper — already an impressive achievement, but not the headline result.
Question 2: does the code compile?
Once you’re convinced that you understand the statement of the theorem which the Lean code purports to prove, you (or perhaps one of your friends who has access to a beefy machine, if the code base is huge) has to actually compile the code.
When Anthropic formalized a proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in Lean, they asked me to take a look at the 13 million lines of code which they had generated. I downloaded it onto my machine, dumped it into a sandbox (because who knows what AI-generated code will do, it can in theory delete all your files) and attempted to compile it; I very quickly ran out of memory. I told Anthropic that I was unable to make any claims about what they had done until I could see the code base compiling, and they gave me temporary access to a machine with 96 cores and 500 gigs of ram. I could then compile the code.
Of course, with a more reasonably-sized codebase it is possible to compile the code on a reasonably-sized machine. For example OpenAI’s resolution of the Navier-Stokes problem is 640K lines of code and compiles fine on my laptop.
It is probably worth stressing again: do not run random Lean code on your local machine unless you sandbox it first. Lean’s mathematics library is safe to run and build upon because this is human-curated and checked by human experts. AI-generated code is not.
Question 3: does the code prove the theorem as stated?
I already talked in Question 1 about the importance of checking the statement of a theorem, so we can be sure that the code is proving the right thing. However, there is an added complication here. Ideally the statement of a theorem will be contained in a file which has very few imports beyond Mathlib, so we know we can trust it. But the proof of the theorem will necessarily import thousands and possibly millions of lines of code which nobody wants to read. How do we know for sure that there is no trick hidden in the millions of lines of proof files which redefines x^n to mean 37, and then proves that a^n + b^n ≠ c^n because the left hand side is 37+37=74 and the right hand side is 37? Or which adds a new axiom to mathematics saying that the theorem is true? Put another way — given a Challenge.lean file with only trusted code imported and the statement of a theorem, and a Solution.lean file with millions of lines of untrusted code imported and the proof of a theorem which looks identical, how do we know for sure that somewhere in the millions of lines of code there is no hack which changes the meaning of the statement, changes the rules from just the axioms of mathematics,  
The one-line answer: lake comparator. You can read more about this answer here. But in short, this tool checks that the theorem stated in a trusted file and the theorem proved via untrusted imports are identical, and that only the axioms of mathematics are used in the proof.
Question 4: does the code exploit a bug in Lean’s official kernel?
This can happen. There was a soundness bug in Lean’s kernel which was fixed four hours after it was discovered, and a subsequent review of Lean’s code base by OpenAI found several more, all of which were fixed before they were announced publicly. There may in theory be more soundness bugs in Lean’s kernel. However, this does not matter.
Why not? Because Lean now has many kernels, created by users, written in many different languages, and at least one of which is formally verified to have no bugs, right down to the assembly level. If you want to make absolutely sure that there is no reward-hacking then again there is a one-line answer: lake comparator --paranoid. A malicious piece of code exploiting an as-yet-undiscovered bug in Lean’s official kernel will not pass this test unless it exploits as-yet-undiscovered bugs in many independent systems all at once. For example this webpage from the Lean kernel arena demonstrates that OpenAI’s resolution of the Navier–Stokes problem is accepted by multiple kernels as well as Lean’s official kernel.
One final remark
Even if the Lean code compiles and passes all these tests, and is thus overwhelmingly likely to be a correct proof of a theorem, this does not mean that any corresponding pdf also contains a correct proof! The Navier–Stokes lost in translation paper demonstrates the opposite in fact, for the Navier-Stokes write-up; whilst all the tests above have been run for the Navier–Stokes work, there are instances where the pdf proof and the Lean proof diverge. In these cases, who knows if the pdf proof is OK! My understanding is that some experts have been using AI to informalise the Lean proof back into English in order to read the argument, rather than ploughing through the slop in the pdf.
Summary/conclusions
“It’s true because it’s checked in Lean” can be made to make sense. But one has to do some work beyond “the Lean code compiles”. Your frontier AI model can do all of this work. But it needs to be done, and (depending on the amount of Lean code in the proof) it may be computationally costly.

Helsing backer Plural raises $1.1B to fund Europe’s next moonshots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-16
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Operator-led VC firm Plural has raised €1 billion ($1.1 billion) in new capital, joining a growing cohort of larger European funds that also includes Mundi Ventures’ Kembara and EQT-managed Scaleup Europe Fund.
Despite its size, Plural’s fundraise isn’t (only) for a growth fund: Two-thirds will go to its third early-stage fund, and one-third to a new “opportunities” fund making select follow-on investments, TechCrunch learned from Plural partners Khaled Helioui and Carina Namih.
The two buckets are fixed, but the check size is not. Plural is “still very committed to being an early-stage fund,” Namih said. But Helioui added that some of the early-stage “moonshots” it plans to back may require “raising a couple hundred million” to get off the ground.
“Moonshot” is an appropriate term to describe some of Plural’s portfolio highlights, such as Proxima Fusion and The Exploration Company — and its new fund will be looking for equally promising opportunities in energy, AI infrastructure, defense, health, and more.
Many of these are capital-intensive, but this is no longer stopping European entrepreneurs, especially second-time founders, and companies like Daniel Ek’s Helsing are “not isolated cases,” said Helioui, who backed the startup’s seed round alongside two Plural partners.
“If you’ve built and scaled a company, chances are, you’re more likely to be driven and passionate about having an impact on Europe’s ability to defend itself, procure its own energy, or own its operations and manufacturing, rather than just another app,” he said.
With bigger pockets, Plural will be able to keep up longer with the larger and larger rounds its portfolio companies have gone on to raise. It also made an effort to raise more of this capital from Europe, Namih said.
While Europe’s institutional LPs were, for a long time, more likely to back banker types than founders hoping to displace those bankers, the current shift toward Europe’s sovereignty and resilience creates tailwinds for Plural, whose office in Tallinn played a key role in its decision to invest in defense tech — including in a missile company, Hypersonica.
“The reality is today still, you have a different level of conversation and a different sense of appreciation of the urgency and the criticality of these topics depending on how far from the border to Russia you are,” said Helioui.
Two of Plural’s six partners are Estonians and Skype alumni: Wise co-founder Taavet Hinrikus and Teleport’s Sten Tamkivi. However, there is more to Plural than Tallinn; the fund also has offices in London, where Helioui, Namih and Ian Hogarth are based, and in Paris, where it hired former Uber executive Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty as a full-time partner in October 2025.
According to a press release, each partner will lead a small number of new investments a year. These companies will then get access to Plural’s growing portfolio support, which already ranges from hiring and communications to finance, Helioui said. That’s another indicator that VC firms in Europe are increasingly starting to look like their U.S. peers.
Pictured from left to right: Ian Hogarth, Taavet Hinrikus, Khaled Helioui, Carina Namih, Sten Tamkivi, and Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty.

Launch failures are always a risk, but amazingly, United Launch Alliance had never experienced one previously. Since the company formed in 2006 as a partnership between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, its Atlas V rocket has been famously dependable. Now, the company's more powerful, more complex Vulcan will be under review by engineers and is facing a possible grounding...
As well as being a major setback for United Launch Alliance, the failed launch will be a blow to Amazon's Leo internet satellite system, intended to rival SpaceXSI's Starlink network. Leo has 38 Vulcan flights booked to launch its satellites, following eight successful Atlas V missions. Many of those are now likely to be delayed.  Amazon's other launch provider, Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin, suffered its own setback in May when its New Glenn rocket exploded on the launchpad.
The Federal Communications Commission required Amazon Leo to have 1,600 satellites in orbit by July 31, 2026, but so far it only has around 390 in service... "No operator could have predicted that all three core heavy-lift launch programs... would experience repeated, concurrent scheduling slips severe enough to exhaust the buffers Amazon Leo had built in," the company said back in July. 
"Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something,"  the company said in a post on X, promising a transparent and thorough investigation.  "We will provide further updates when new information becomes available.
